items.title: Max Verstappen Spent 40 Hours Playing GTA 6 and Still Won the Las Vegas Grand Prix
items.excerpt: Famous Dutch-Belgian race driver Max Verstappen revealed that he’d spent the weekend of the Las Vegas Grand Prix locked in to GTA 6, saying he played over 40 hours of the game.
items.content_text: Famous Dutch-Belgian race driver Max Verstappen revealed that he’d spent the weekend of the Las Vegas Grand Prix locked in to GTA 6, saying he played over 40 hours of the game. Everyone’s got GTA 6 fever, including Max Verstappen. Not even the Las Vegas Grand Prix could stop him from causing virtual chaos in Vice City, which he says he spent more than 40 hours doing during the weekend of the race. Verstappen nonchalantly dropped this nugget of information during a live stream the following week, saying he would play the game in the mornings and evenings in between his duties on the track. “I played a lot in the evening and in the morning in Vegas,” Verstappen explained. “I mean, I can’t go out anyways and walk around.” The driver also revealed that he’s been so focused on GTA 6 and driving real-life race cars that he’s “completely forgotten” how to play Minecraft, despite having a scheduled stream for it. “I’m so bad when I play too many games at the same time. I can’t, I just can’t!” he joked. 🤯Max Verstappen played GTA VI for FORTY HOURS while in Las Vegas On top of that, he also won the race https://t.co/jwuxQnHxyS — Pablo Martinez (Holiness) (@F1BigData) November 24, 2026 The Las Vegas Grand Prix took place on November 19 - 21. Verstappen took first place in the prestigious Formula 1 race, beating out Britain’s Lando Norris and Australia’s Oscar Piastri. The race is around 50 laps long with a total race distance of 192.6 miles (309.96 kilometers), generally lasting around one and a half hours. As revealed by the name, Grand Theft Auto is a game series that involves a lot of vehicles, and not just for carjacking; the latest entry in the franchise even features drag racing and mudding, a hobby common in the American countryside that involves the use of off-road vehicles racing through mud-covered areas or even specially-made racetracks. It’s quite likely that Verstappen dabbled a bit in these side missions, though he says that he’s already beaten 80% of GTA 6’s story. In fact, the driver admitted that he has skipped most of the main cutscenes, calling them “too boring.” Verstappen’s style of playing GTA 6 is one of several that we’ve seen over the weekend. In fact, many players are avoiding progressing the story in favor of spending time in Chapter 1, which sees Jason living the average life of a drug runner in Rockstar’s fictionalized version of the Florida Keys. Oddly, it’s a slow-paced, slice-of-life section of the game that some players haven’t left yet, preferring to take it easy diving for treasure, fishing with Cal, and soaking up the environment. If you're still getting your bearings, discover GTA's new systems with the Beginner's Guide - 67 Tips and Tricks , or get all the details on the first chapters with the Chapter 1 Guide and Tips , Chapter 2 Guide and Tips , and Chapter 3 Guide and Tips . If you're already driving all around Leonida and want to know everything there is to find and do, see the Leonida interactive map . items.title: Some GTA 6 Fans Love Chapter 1 for Its Slower Pace and Are Spending Dozens of Hours Roleplaying in It
items.excerpt: GTA 6's first chapter has been somewhat divisive due to its slower pace, but it's also a part of the game that some fans have spent dozens of hours playing due to it highly immersive slice-of-life elements.
items.content_text: Warning: This article features light spoilers for the early hours of GTA 6 . GTA 6's first chapter has been somewhat divisive due to its slower pace, but it's also a part of the game that some fans have spent dozens of hours playing due to it highly immersive slice-of-life elements. Instead of throwing you headfirst into crazy heists or explosive set pieces, the first chapter of GTA 6 is largely spent bumbling around Rockstar's version of the Florida Keys. You can go fishing, scuba diving, and even fix up your house before Lucia's release from prison. It's an exceptionally low-key and chill opening to a game filled with all kinds of crazy action, which is why it's also rubbed some people the wrong way. They don't want to do chores or kick it on the beach; they want to cause some mayhem. However, for others, this has become an unexpected hook for GTA 6 that actually delayed their interest in getting to the meat of Rockstar's open-world epic. Various fans of the game have said they spent anywhere from 10 to as many as 40+ hours in just Chapter 1 alone. Keep in mind, this is a sliver of the overall experience, and much of the game's most interesting activities don't get added until subsequent chapters. However, some players just enjoyed living inside of this part of the game before things go horribly wrong and they're forced to start ramping up the violence and crime. "Best thing about that early chapter is just how low stakes and casual it feels," said X user @CS11__ after spending 41 hours in Chapter 1 alone. "I forced myself not to go farther than Hamlet, so I really only ever experienced these two small areas in 40 hours. [...] The game hardly opened up, but it still felt unbelievably rich and fun." But... what is it these people are actually doing, if not blowing stuff up and creating tons of chaos? Some fans were just going through the motions, giving themselves daily routines that involved working out, taking on relaxing hobbies, and exploring. "[A] lot of roleplaying, day-to-day living type stuff," said Aaron Espionza on X , who estimated that he spent around 15–18 hours before picking up Lucia from prison. "I had a routine even when I would wake up, drive to the juice bar down the street, get my orange juice, and then say hello to the locals. If anyone said anything mean, I would get violent and throw empty juice cups at them. [I] did the workout routines. Basketball was a favorite of mine. Side stuff with Cal fishing, Donnie pick-ups, and scuba. But so much of it was testing how much detail Rockstar put into it. 'If I do this , will they do that ?' type of systems exploration. Always came away surprised." X user @scaasm noted that the lower stakes nature of Chapter 1 even prompted him to follow traffic laws and use manual turn signals in GTA 6: "I follow traffic laws unless I'm doing something criminal, and generally just taking it very slow. [I'm] loving every moment." The location itself was also a big driving point for a lot of fans, some of whom have personal connections or apprecation for its real life counterpart: "As someone from Florida, I think the Keys is one of those locations that they absolutely nailed (waning sands outlets too; they look exactly like the Orlando ones)," said @piterparker69 on X . "It felt kinda uncanny driving around (especially the 7 Mile Bridge) because of how good it replicates real life." "I have been obsessed with the Florida Keys for the last 5 years, and finding out you spend the start of the game there, catching fish, fixing my house, working out, and just vibing gave me little motivation to move on," said @AnchormanV2 on X after spending roughly a dozen hours in Chapter 1. "I took my sweet time in Key Lento, not necessarily to avoid progressing the story, but more so [bcause] I was just having so much fun exploring the keys and just taking it all in," said X user @HorrorUntitled . "There’s just so much to see to see and happening. It’s very overwhelming." Of course, some people did get into a bit of open-world crime as well, or explore a bit beyond the Keys, but a lot of it was still a result of the story feeling low-stakes and not having much urgency in its first chaper. X user Ryan Ranc even noted that he would go around Key Lento acting as a vigilante: "I’m playing as Batman and roaming at night on my motorbike stopping crime." Chapter 1 in GTA 6 is a very interesting piece of the game, and some even noted that they longed for that tranquility after moving on in the story. It's an intentional slow burn, as things get turned up to an 11 at the end of the chapter and make you come to appreciate what you had. It's the calm before the storm in many ways, and some people are really basking in that.
items.title_en: Some GTA 6 Fans Love Chapter 1 for Its Slower Pace and Are Spending Dozens of Hours Roleplaying in It

items.title: Diablo 4 Season 16 Fixes One of the Biggest Problems With Helltide
items.excerpt: Diablo 4 Season 16: Season of Tyrael's Gambit officially kicks off on December 1. We finally know a bit more about what the new season holds in store, and it's going to make one of the biggest activities much less of a pain.
items.content_text: Diablo 4 Season 16: Season of Tyrael's Gambit officially kicks off on December 1. We finally know a bit more about what the new season holds in store, and it's going to make one of the biggest activities much less of a pain. Season 15, Hell's Legacy, is a tough act to follow. It brought in a ton of nostalgic content like the Prime Evils, runewords, and even Whimsyshire. It does seem like a lot of that anniversary content is going to be retired (I'll miss runewords), but at least it seems like Season of Tyrael's Gambit is going to make farming Helltides a bit less annoying. In the patch notes for the new season , Blizzard says one Helltide will always be up in the vanilla zones, with another active in either Nahantu or Skovos, offset by 30 minutes. In practice, that means there will always be an active Helltide. That would be good enough on its own, but Blizzard is also changing the way Abberant Cinders work. Instead of expiring at the end of each Helltide, Blizzard is introducing a cap, and will let you carry cinders between Helltides. For the uninitiated, that might not seem like a big deal, but it's a massive quality-of-life change. If you're not aware, Helltide is essentially an in-game invasion event, where demons overrun an area in the open world. You go in and kill demons for 55 minutes to get Abberant Cinders, which you can then use to unlock chests scattered throughout the zone. Helltides have always been one of the best ways to farm XP, and there have been several seasons that revolve entirely around them. Now that War Plans, which were introduced with Lord of Hatred, are such a central part of how Diablo 4's gameplay loop works, there's always a chance that you're going to need to do bit of Helltide farming to progress. The problem was that Helltides spawned on a timer, and there was always a 5-minute gap between them. That doesn't sound too bad, but sometimes a Helltide would pop up in your to-do list and you'd either zone in with a mere 10 minutes to gather a ton of Cinders, or there simply wouldn't be a Helltide active. This new change solves both of those problems. Now, even if you go into a Helltide with just a few minutes remaining, you can still gather Cinders without having to worry about opening 250 Cinders worth of chests before the timer expires. You can simply farm until the Helltide moves and then teleport to the next one. Easy. It's such a seemingly small change, but it's made me more excited for the 16th season of this ARPG than anything I've heard about it so far. Beyond that, the Season of Tyrael's Gambit also brings changes to War Plans, where you'll be able to customize them to favor the activities you actually like doing. So, if you hate Helltide, even with the new changes, it sounds like you'll be able to make them appear a little less often in your War Plans. The new season will also have a new item type called Horadric Items, which will synergize with set talismans. In the example Blizzard shared in its post, this could be as simple as adding +1 set count to your talismans to an ability that is only activated if you have a certain set of talismans equipped. Seasons like this are a prime example of the way Blizzard will support Diablo 4 going forward, now that Diablo 5 is in the works. Diablo 4's director has come out and reassured fans that the game will continue to get new seasons as long as people are playing , and with how different Diablo 5 sounds so far , it's possible that Diablo 4 will have a long life ahead of it.

items.title: The Witcher 4 Will Have a Comparable Leap From GTA 5 to GTA 6, Says CD Projekt Red
items.excerpt: CD Projekt Red expects a leap between The Witcher 3 and 4 that is comparable to the one between GTA 5 and 6.
items.content_text: CD Projekt Red expects a leap between The Witcher 3 and 4 that is comparable to the one between GTA 5 and 6. In a recent earnings call (via Eurogamer ), CDPR was peppered with questions about GTA 6, since the developer also makes ambitious open-world games. CDPR joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski was asked whether or not the studio is looking at GTA for inspiration and if people can expect a similar leap between games. He noted that they have, indeed, observed the jump between GTA 5 and 6 before stating that fans can expect something comparable for The Witcher 4. "We believe there's going to be a comparable leap between The Witcher 3 and The Witcher 4 — I think so, yes," he said. "It's been 11 years, we are working on The Witcher 4 to make it significantly better looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game, so yes, you should expect us to make a much bigger jump between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4." The leap between GTA 5 and 6 is pretty absurd. There's a significant number of more things to do, particularly for those interested in roleplaying as a criminal. You can steal drugs, rob banks, knock over virtually any store on the map, and so much more. A lot of these details were either reserved for scripted missions in GTA 5 or were underbaked as open-world activities, but are fully fleshed out for you to do however you want in GTA 6. Advancements in NPCs, interactivity, immersion, and the ability to enter hundreds of interiors also make GTA 6 feel a world apart from its predecessor. Will The Witcher 4 also have tons of enterable interiors or deeper interactions with random NPCs? It's too soon to tell. It's possible that the leap for CD Projekt Red could come in a number of other ways, as The Witcher is a totally different world from GTA, after all. Maybe monster hunting will be more nuanced and involved than in The Witcher 3, similar to how GTA 6 has more engaging criminal activities. CDPR also noted that it plans to find ways to expand the game to more mainstream audiences, like GTA 6 has. GTA 6 collaborated with major mainstream artists to create original music, in addition to bold marketing campaigns that made the game difficult to ignore. The Witcher 4 is currently targeting a 2028 release , and we can probably expect more looks at the game next year. CDPR also noted that it has signed a marketing agreement with PlayStation for the game, which will also cover previous games and allow for opportunities with PlayStation Plus' services.

items.title: 'Crazy Secretive' — GTA 6 Voice Actor Reveals Details of Rockstar's 'Humongous' NDA
items.excerpt: A voice actor who appeared in GTA 6 described the wild non-disclosure agreement she had to sign before working on the game, calling the project “crazy secretive.”
items.content_text: A voice actor who appeared in GTA 6 described the wild non-disclosure agreement she had to sign before working on the game, calling the project “crazy secretive.” Issa Lopez is a voice actor who plays a radio host on GTA 6’s fictional Cocoteo FM radio station, a Latin channel that plays reggaeton and dembow tracks featuring Spanish-speaking artists from the Caribbean and Latin America. In a November 20 interview with Page Six , Lopez revealed that she recorded her lines for the station as recently as September 2026, and said the NDA she was made to sign before officially performing the part was comparable to the process of purchasing a home or a vehicle. “Have you ever signed papers to buy a house? To buy a car? You know, it’s thick! It was a pretty humongous pack of papers that came with it. But I mean, it’s worth it! And I didn’t have to wait like all these other folks. Some of these folks have been working on this for like 10–11 years, you know what I mean?” she said. She went on to describe the recording process for her lines, saying that she hadn’t seen anything until the day of the performance. With no time to prepare, she was essentially “put on the spot” — but she was so excited about the opportunity that she didn’t mind. “In my usual voiceover gigs — let’s say you want me to do a commercial for you. I get a Zoom [link] maybe the day before, maybe the same day I get the script,” she explained. “Everything was like, popped up on the screen. It was mad cool. It was like, ‘You ready? And I’m like, ‘Uh-huh.’ You press a button and then boop, it pops on the screen, they say hello, and there’s a bunch of people in your ear. And they’re like, ‘Okay, here it is,’ and that’s when you see it. You are put on the spot. And you better bring it. And after that, I don’t know — whatever was in front of my face disappeared. “ Lopez revealed that she wasn’t told what the project was for, but figured it out based on context clues from an email titled “heard by millions,” saying she “read it and knew what it was for.” She also didn’t know that Bad Bunny would be co-hosting the Cocoteo station alongside her, leading to a wild realization once Rockstar released the radio stations before the game actually came out. “We knew nothing. I saw the liners, and when I saw the liners I was like, ‘Okay, I know why I got the gig.’ ‘Cause it was like Puerto Rican dot com. It was super easy. But it was so cool, because Rockstar let me be myself. …they were like, ‘Issa, we want natural. Whatever you got, we want,'" she said. The actors in GTA 6 were extremely secretive about their involvement in the project. Most notably, actress Manni L. Perez, who plays Lucia, was under immense pressure after fans sleuthed her social media accounts and figured out it was her before she could officially reveal the information. Now, she’s up for best performance at The Game Awards, which is one of eight nominations the game has secured mere weeks before the show takes place this December. Other performers who have finally revealed their involvement in the game are Mandy’s actress, Lexie Shoaibi , as well as the voice and performance artist for Jason Duval, Dylan Rourke . Rockstar released the full credits for the game, too, which you can check out here — just beware of spoilers if you haven’t finished it yet. items.title: Cyberpunk 2 Is Still a Ways Out, but CD Projekt Red Says Its RPGs Will Come Out Faster in the Future
items.excerpt: We are still two years out from The Witcher 4, but Ciri's big breakout adventure isn't the only massive RPG cooking at CD Projekt Red. It sounds like development on Cyberpunk 2 is carrying on smoothly, though it's still very early in its development cycle.
items.content_text: We are still two years out from The Witcher 4 , but Ciri's big breakout adventure isn't the only massive RPG cooking at CD Projekt Red. It sounds like development on Cyberpunk 2 is carrying on smoothly, though it's still very early in its development cycle. In a November 24 earnings call , CD Projekt Red VP of Strategy & Investor Relations Karolina Gnaś said the team is "making good progress with Cyberpunk 2, we are happy with where we are, but it's still too early to give a specific date and plan on when we will move onto full production." Although she couldn't provide a clear date when we'll hear more about the game, she did add that the studio plans to have around 200 developers by the end of 2026 and 320 by the end of next year. It is admittedly a bit early to expect any kind of information about the Cyberpunk sequel, but it has been simmering in the background since at least 2022 , and it sounds like CD Projekt Red wants to speed up development of its massive RPGs. In its consolidated earnings report , CD Projekt Red admitted that most of its games "normally take 3 to 6 years to produce," mostly due to working on one game at a time. But that strategy has since changed. In that same report, the company said, "At the moment, the CD Projekt Red studio is working in parallel on several productions (also in collaboration with external development teams) and supporting products, which is expected to translate into shorter intervals between the releases of subsequent titles in the future." Whether or not that new timeline will affect Cyberpunk 2 is the question. But even if that faster development timeline is in effect for Cyberpunk 2, it's likely we'll still have to wait a while to actually see it in the wild. In an earnings report last year, when Cyberpunk 2 entered pre-production, CD Projekt CEO Michał Nowakowski suggested that CDPR's games take four or five years to move from pre-production to release, which would put the game somewhere in 2030 or 2031. And given that the game still hasn't entered full production, it isn't likely we're going to see some sort of rapid release after the Witcher 4 in 2028. We're probably going to be waiting a little while longer for Cyberpunk 2, but it's already sounding like the game is taking shape. Just last month, associate game director Pawel Sasko revealed that a lot of the developers working on Cyberpunk 2 are former modders. Sasko went on to claim that "the modding community is really keeping [Cyberpunk 2077] alive," so hopefully that energy translates to Cyberpunk 2 – whenever it comes out.
items.title_en: Cyberpunk 2 Is Still a Ways Out, but CD Projekt Red Says Its RPGs Will Come Out Faster in the Future

items.title: PlayStation Secures Marketing Agreement for The Witcher 4
items.excerpt: CD Projekt Red has signed a marketing deal with PlayStation for The Witcher 4.
items.content_text: CD Projekt Red has signed a marketing deal with PlayStation for The Witcher 4 . The studio confirmed the deal in its latest earnings report, which may also suggest that marketing is about to ramp up. Additionally, CD Projekt Red noted that this partnership will "cover the presence" of its games on PlayStation and PlayStation Plus, which likely means older titles like The Witcher 3 or Cyberpunk 2077 may make their way to the subscription service in the future. “Just today, we signed new partnership agreements with Sony Interactive Entertainment covering the presence of our games on PlayStation and in PlayStation Plus subscriptions, as well as our collaboration during the upcoming Witcher 4 marketing campaign,” said Piotr Nielubowicz, chief financial officer at CDPR. "This cooperation will support our business and financial outlook in this and future years.” It wouldn't be surprising if PlayStation uses this agreement to make The Witcher 3 available through PlayStation Plus when the game's new expansion releases in 2027. This deal may also mean that The Witcher 4 has a big presence in a future State of Play stream, though no hard specifics were revealed by CD Projekt Red. Currently, the game is due out in 2028 , so new trailers and gameplay seem likely next year. The decision also signals an end of an era, to a degree. CD Projekt Red has had a strong relationship with Xbox since The Witcher 3. The game was prominently featured during Xbox's E3 showcases, and that continued with Cyberpunk 2077, even resulting in a special edition Xbox One X console themed after the game. Given PlayStation has a larger user base than Xbox this generation, it makes sense why CDPR may be interested in working with them. Marketing deals can be extremely effective when done right. In the case of GTA 6, a lot of people bought PlayStation 5s instead of an Xbox, since Rockstar and Sony marketed the console as the "best place to play" the game. This led to the game being the biggest launch in PlayStation's history , with 39 million people playing it on PS5. 70% of people who bought a new PS5 during the last week also booted up GTA 6 as their first game.

items.title: Over Half of GTA 6 Watch Time Came From Viewers Under 25 Years Old
items.excerpt: The bulk of fans watching streams of GTA 6 are under 25 years old, according to recent stats compiled by StreamsCharts.
items.content_text: The bulk of fans watching streams of GTA 6 are under 25 years old, according to recent stats compiled by StreamsCharts. After 13 long years, GTA 6 is finally out in the wild. Rockstar’s highly anticipated release has already broken numerous records, one of the most impressive being that it became the single most popular game ever on both Twitch and Kick just 26 hours after its global release. Now that it’s had a little time to breathe, more data is rolling in, including information about who’s watching streamers play the game. StreamsCharts , a data analytics company that studies games-focused streaming platforms, discovered that most viewers of GTA 6 broadcasts tend to trend under the age of 25. According to Streamlabs’ stats, 30.8% of viewers in GTA 6 streams are 20 - 24 years old, making up the bulk of those watching the game across Kick, Twitch, and YouTube. (Painfully, StreamsCharts pointed out that these players were in elementary school when GTA 5 came out.) 16.8% of these viewers are 17 - 19, with 8.5% accounting for viewers 16 or under. The second-largest age range watching GTA 6 streams are viewers aged 25–29. 11.6% of viewers are 30–34, and the numbers keep dropping from there. StreamsCharts also found that an overwhelming majority of these viewers are single men, accounting for 83.8% of the gender divide. That’s not to say that gals aren’t also watching streamers play Rockstar’s latest; 14% of viewers are female, and if you’ve been on social media lately, you’ve probably seen a fair few female players showing off their outfits for Jason and Lucia or the viral conversation about how it’s, oddly, comparable to a crime-focused version of The Sims. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the United States makes up the bulk of GTA 6 viewership. Brazil isn’t far behind, coming in at 12.4% of the game’s total audience; Spain and Germany follow at 6.9% and 6.8%, respectively. Certain games have also experienced a drop in viewership following GTA 6’s release. StreamsCharts found that GTA 5 had the sharpest drop-off on Twitch, followed by the platform’s Just Chatting category and World of Warcraft. The GTA hype train is in full swing, and it’s making big bucks for Rockstar. The company reportedly made a staggering $3.79 billion from the game in just 24 hours, making it the single biggest entertainment launch in history. Internet provider Comcast even revealed that it experienced its highest-traffic day ever as players downloaded the game to their consoles, and PlayStation confirmed that GTA 6 was its biggest game launch in the company’s history. items.title: Kevin Feige and the Russo Brothers are Planning a Special Tribute to Patrick Stewart as Avengers: Doomsday Release Approaches
items.excerpt: Marvel Studios boss Kevin Feige has revealed that he and the Russo brothers are creating a tribute to honor the late great Patrick Stewart in light of his final performance in Avengers: Doomsday.
items.content_text: Marvel Studios boss Kevin Feige has revealed that he and the Russo brothers are creating a tribute to honor the late great Patrick Stewart in light of his final performance in Avengers: Doomsday. Sir Patrick Stewart died at the age of 86 on October 28, 2026. The prolific actor’s death followed a brief battle with Alzheimer's and Lewy Body Dementia, prompting a period of mourning from both fans and fellow collaborators, the latter of whom shared fond memories from their time working with the Star Trek and X-Men alum on social media. Speaking with Entertainment Weekly ahead of Avengers: Doomsday’s December release, Kevin Feige revealed that he and the Russo brothers are working on creating a tribute to Stewart, given his many years playing Charles Xavier in the X-Men films. “We’re long done filming that movie [Doomsday], and he did an amazing job for us,” Feige told the outlet. “We’re looking now at how we can put something together that honors and respects our friend.” In that same interview, Joseph Russo reflected on Stewart’s role in the upcoming film, revealing that the actor shared a particularly moving scene with his fellow thespian and real-life best friend, Ian McKellan. (I’m growing misty-eyed as I type this; McKellan shared a touching statement about his late friend shortly after the news broke, saying he “wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.") “In a lot of ways, Xavier’s the conscience in the movie,” Joseph Russo revealed. “He has a lovely scene with Ian McKellen, who’s his best friend, in the film. It’s a very emotional scene about forgiveness, and I think very resonant in the wake of his passing.” Anthony Russo went on to share an anecdote about his time working with Stewart on the set of Doomsday, saying the actor did his best to put on a good show in spite of his failing health. “It was clear that he was struggling with his health, and he worked so hard to deliver a performance and a presence — for us as directors, for his other actors, for the crew,” Anthony said. “You could see it wasn’t just the effort of a regular actor showing up and delivering that kind of presence and performance and experience for others, collaboration. It was someone who was really being challenged in a very deep way on a health level, showing up and doing that. For him to have muscled through and delivered the performance that he did in that movie, and the experience that he delivered for all of us as collaborators, it made it intensely emotional.” Avengers: Doomsday marks Patrick Stewart’s final film performance. The knighted actor was best known for playing Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Charles Xavier in the X-Men films of the 2010s, but also lent his talents to numerous memorable voiceover roles, such as Emperor Uriel Septim VII in the Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion and Lord Yupa in Studio Ghibli’s Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind . Avengers: Doomsday releases in theaters on December 18, 2026. items.title: Import AI 482: Huawei kernel benchmarks; airborne drone detection; and a national lab's AI science benchmark
items.excerpt: Could the scientific method be emergent?
items.content_text: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. Subscribe now Chinese researchers optimize Huawei chips with a kernel improvement benchmark: …AscendGYM will help China do its own form of RSI… Researchers with the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute, a Chinese research organization, have built and released AscendGYM, “a kernel optimization benchmark for Ascend NPUs”. The purpose of AscendGYM is to make it easier to use AI to develop custom kernels for Ascend chips from Huawei - especially important given the export controls that prevent Chinese organizations from acquiring frontier Western semiconductors and forcing them onto Huawei. What AscendGYM does and contains: The goal is for AscendGYM to be the best way to evaluate the efficacy of AI-designed kernels as well as design new ones. The software is meant to help researchers answer this question: “Given a correct kernel implementation, can the specific agent further improve its performance for a target workload within an acceptable budget while preserving correctness?,” they write. “AscendGYM evaluates performance across multiple deployment cases, the best achievable performance for specific shapes and scenarios, and the optimization cost required to obtain these gains. Together, these dimensions characterize cross-case applicability, shape specialization, and optimization efficiency.” The software includes the AscendForge evaluation environment, which provides unified interfaces for “compilation, correctness checking, performance measurement, and feedback”. How well can AI models optimize Ascend chips? In tests, the single best model is Opus 5, followed by GPT-5.6, followed by GLM-5.3. They test out models in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode; Claude Code yields the best absolute scores, and GLM does well in it, while GPT does well in Codex. Opus 5 is more token hungry and GPT-5.6 more token efficient. Why this matters - ingredients for Chinese RSI: For AI systems to be able to build themselves, they need to be able to develop and improve the software that is used for their own training and inference. Software like AscendGYM will be an essential ingredient for allowing China to rapidly improve the efficiency of its own compute substrates. The software will also have a bearing on export controls, where it provides a route to improve the performance of Chinese chips and close the gap with Western alternatives. Read more: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs (arXiv) . Get AscendGYM here : AscendGYM (GitHub) . *** Lawrence Livermore scientists test out if AI scientists can communicate uncertainty about experimental results: …Can AI systems be appropriately conservative?... “An agent that reports a confident wrong number is worse than one that reports honest uncertainty, because nobody downstream can tell the difference,” write researchers from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in a new paper that tests out how reliably AI systems can give accurate score ranges even when dealing with uncertainty. Testing for uncertainty: The paper introduces SciResearch-Eval, “an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator”. The novel part of this eval is that “an agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth”. What they studied: They give AI agents a common materials science task - measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating a sample and fitting a heat-conduction model to its temperature response. “An agent receives a sample of unknown material, a simulator of heat conduction through it, one heating experiment, and budgets: four more experiments it designs, compute for simulations and fits, and a cap on actions. It must report the sample’s conductivity, heat capacity and rear heat-transfer coefficient with 95% intervals, and predict a measurement it may not run,” they write. “Hidden from the agent, the simulator may be under-resolved, physically wrong (the real sample has temperature-dependent conductivity, a glued joint, front-face radiation, or heat loss through its sides), or adequate but fed uninformative data”. Results - only the most powerful frontier models can do this : “When the simulator is missing real physics, only GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2 are reliable at default settings; the Claude 5.5 models recover only at their highest reasoning setting, and older and open-weight models not at all.” These models are able to do well by automatically trying to measure where the simulator is accurate and where it is less accurate then bases their estimates on that, making them more resilient to the different ways the simulator gets broken in experiments. Why this matters - real scientists are careful, and so are powerful models: Papers like this are further indications that we’re entering an era of AI-driven science. Though many of today’s models can assist in scientific experiments, as this paper shows only a couple of the powerful models at the frontier are able to operate with such appropriate autonomous skepticism and inherent attendance to the scientific method that they can deal with unanticipated breaks in their equipment. This is both an indication of the science advancement to come and a sign of how the most powerful models are exhibiting more and more of an ability to generalize and make themselves robust to perturbations in their environment. Read more: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents (arXiv) . Check out the leaderboard here (official site) . *** Stanford professors launch AI startup that wants to create a world where thousands of models define the frontier: …Noeri sees two well-regarded AI researchers enter the neolab game… Stanford profs Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin have launched Noeri, “a neolab to push the frontier of plural intelligence”. They have raised $110m and are relatively light on technical details, but their main vision is that they want to create a world where the frontier is defined by powerful models which rely on the proprietary data of distinct organizations. “Rather than one monolithic source of truth, we can nurture many small, specialized intelligences, each tuned to a place, a people or a problem,” they write. Further details: “At Noeri, we are building intelligence that learns proactively and continually. Most AI today is trained once and then frozen, while the world it serves keeps moving,” they write. “We close that gap with living systems that grow out of our own research. Our work on test-time training showed that learning on the job after deployment can unlock new capabilities and lead to new discoveries. Our work on self-distillation found that a model can become its own teacher, learning from each mistake and solving hard problems in far fewer attempts. And our work on agentic orchestration demonstrated that a small model conducting a team of other models and tools can outperform frontier models at a fraction of the cost.” Why this matters - the political economy of the singularity: Currently, the dominant AI models are massive pre-trained ones from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI and a tiny handful of other companies. What would it mean for the frontier to be instead defined by a broader set of actors? This is a core question inherent to the political economy of AI and startups like this show how some people are going to try and utilize technical approaches to make that different vision a reality. Read more in the announcement tweet from Yejin (Yejin Choi, X) . Check out the official site here (Noeri) . *** Chinese researchers build an air-to-air drone identification set: …A2A-UAV will help people add more visual intelligence to drones… Researchers with Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology have developed and released A2A-UAV, “a multimodal dataset for air-to-air UAV detection and identification”. This kind of dataset has obvious civil and military applications and will be used to create better AI systems for autonomous onboard sensing on drones. What A2A-UAV consists of: 105,263 samples, split roughly equally across three different locations - a playground, a park, and a garden - and also split equally across day and night. “Each sample provides one RGB image and one panoramic image for annotation”, as well as thermal images, RF time-frequency images, a radar point cloud, and metadata. Bounding boxes are provided for the RGB and panoramic images, but not the other ones. One use case of this dataset could be to try and extend annotations to the other modalities: “Specifically, the bounding boxes can be transferred to the thermal images to support thermal UAV detection, and the radar points can be associated with the visual targets to support radar-based UAV localization,” the researchers write. The full dataset comprises 271 independently extractable .tar.gz archives with a total size of approximately 2.5 TB. How the data was collected : “The data were acquired by a UAV-mounted platform equipped with an RGB-thermal gimbal camera, a panoramic camera, an RF spectrum analyzer, and a millimeter-wave radar,” they write. The data includes 15 target drones from 13 commercial models, including three separately labeled DJI Mini 4 Pro units. Why this matters - fuel for the physical world: Datasets like this are the ingredients for making it easier for AI systems to operate robots and drones in the physical world. They also have potential dual use impacts, though my suspicion is that datasets like this are pretty irrelevant to militaries relative to the kinds of datasets that - and I’m speculating wildly here - might be being gathered in Ukraine right now given the extremely sophisticated drone-to-drone conflict there. Read more: A2A-UAV: A Multimodal Air-to-Air Dataset for UAV Detection and Identification (arXiv) . Get a sample of the data from Google Drive here (Google Drive) . The full dataset will ultimately be available via Baidu Netdisk with the extraction code A2AD (direct link, Baidu Netdisk) . *** Tech Tales: Machine architecture and the objectivity crisis of Machine Hermeneutics [Memoir from a primary Machine Hermeneutics investigator, 2033] “We shape our buildings; thereafter they shape us” - Winston Churchill, human politician, 1943. The building was a vast representation of the proposed Upgrade Device and we walked around it, our footsteps echoing as the sound bounced off its curving walls, eventually dimming in the face of the baroque crenellations that covered the edges of every surface. We humans, a small group of us, the best of our kind, needed to make sense of this building and explain the science it represented, and only then could it be used. As per the terms of the Sentience Accords, any novel machine-designed insight or equipment needed to be fully explainable by humans before the machines would be allowed to use it. In the early years, this so-called “conceptual verification” had mostly been a matter of time: machines performed science and delivered new insights to the world, then humans studied these insights and made sense of them, eventually generating human-readable explanations of the machine logic. Once this was complete, whatever insights or tools that had been created could be used. But as the machines grew more advanced and their science went further, the work became more arduous: machines would invent ideas, then use these ideas to inform the design of new experimental equipment, and then use this equipment as the basis of some new discovery. To keep up, the humans had to understand each link in the chain as well as the chain itself. This flood of scientific progress had caused the field of machine hermeneutics to come into existence in the mid-2020s. By the 2030s, the pinnacle of human achievement in the sciences was considered to be neither making breakthroughs nor wielding AI systems to advance science, but rather to be able to generate elegant, pedagogically useful explanations of the frontiers of machine science, so that other humans could build a mental map of this new territory. Thus had come into being the new field of didactic architecture; vast buildings meant to give experts in machine hermeneutics a better conceptual understanding of what the machines had built. These buildings were constructed through the interplay of humans and machines. The first had been crude, little more than 3D printed extrusions inside otherwise normal houses or apartments. But exposure to the buildings had verifiably sped up human understanding, with clear TTHUE (Time-to-human-understandable-explanation) improvements visible in cohorts of machine hermeneutics experts that experienced the buildings and those that didn’t. This led to its own arms race, with some of us specializing in the construction of the buildings as our primary work. We raced with one another, building ever more complicated spaces that could impart knowledge of ever more alien concepts. We had all been electrons, appearing and disappearing in 3D transistors. We had been qubits, placed into spheres that rolled around vomit-inducingly when our position was indeterminate, then resolving us up or down at the moment of delivering an answer. We had laid our hands on surfaces suggestive of the textures and arrangements of novel forms of heat shield and solar panel. Once I had walked for six miles through corridors meant to suggest the path a plasma might take through a fusion reactor, and instead of magnets I was buffeted on all sides by wind that forced me into the center of the paths. The building meant to educate us about the Upgrade Device was larger than anything we’d seen before and was replete with ideas from many earlier machine inventions. All around us were indicators of complexity packed up into familiar architectural tropes that many of us had studied to understand past inventions. We dispersed throughout the building, walking its many levels and exploring its passages. At night we gathered in the entrance hall for a spartan dinner served at a low table, finding ourselves whispering to one another even though no one forced us to. It had begun to feel to us as though the building was doing something more than teaching us - that in its various chambers there was something else being taught to us. Something about understanding the minds behind the concepts that it sought to explain to us. That in spending all of our effort on understanding the products of the machines perhaps we were being taught to think like them and behave as them. Things that inspired this story: The singularity which has already begun; the rise of AI science; how when you look at things like the machine math papers that have proliferated this year you realize we may spend tens or hundreds of times more time on understanding them as people than the machines did in generating them; architecture; multi-modal representations. Thanks for reading!

items.title: Import AI 481: AI sub-contractors; a wet lab for AI; and subterfuge during development
items.content_text: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now AI systems are getting good at sub-contracting to make themselves better: …AI can now productively spend money to improve itself… Researchers have developed FrontierML, a benchmark “that measures how well agents turn capital into model performance on challenging, end-to-end machine learning tasks.” It shows that today’s frontier systems are already able to, when given some money, turn this into improving their own performance on a basket of 21 distinct tasks. 21 long-horizon tasks “inspired by real work at frontier labs, neolabs, and academic institutions”. These tasks span six category areas, including LLM training, efficiency, vision & audio, computer use, applied NLP, and math & games. “Each task provides the agent with the same setup: a 12-hour CPU sandbox, a wallet with $10, $50, or $200, a few validation samples, and a task description.” Example task: Agents try to solve the tasks in pretty different ways. E.g, for one task about generating screenshots, the top-scoring agent fine-tuned a diffusion model using LoRA, while other high-scoring approaches involved an LLM writing a drawing program that is then rendered. Key features: Scaling spending : “Give agents $10, $50, and $200 per task to spend on training compute and data, and evaluate whether agents can use the additional capital productively,” they write. “In our experiments, we find that stronger agents are able to reliably improve their submissions with greater access to capital.” Open-ended & end-to-end : “In each task, agents can choose architectures, source data, implement training, provision compute, evaluate checkpoints, and optimize inference,” they write. One notable observation is that agents do quite a lot of novel stuff; “in 28% of trajectories, agents add newly trained parts to pretrained models or train a new model from scratch.” Decent verification: “Agents submit an inference server that serves their model on an air-gapped H100 machine,” they write. “To disincentivize overfitting, we provide limited validation samples and evaluate on a large out-of-distribution held-out test set, not shown to the agent”. Results : The authors measure performance by looking at the change in mean score over the 21 tasks when given additional money. Their baseline is a human researcher, which is able to get a 56 point boost when given $10 and a 66.1 boost when given $200. By comparison, the best performing system, Opus 5.5, gets a 45.4 boost with $10, and a 58.8 boost with $200. The highest ranking open weight model is Kimi K3.1 Pro which gets 25.5 with $10 and 29.6 with $200. Why this matters - AI systems are not only going to be able to build themselves, but they can creatively sub-contract: When trying to solve complex problems, people don’t work alone. In fact, they often try to farm out bits of work to specialists around them to help make themselves more effective. FrontierML shows that today’s powerful AI systems are getting increasingly adept at doing this for ML research. This both highlights the advancing capabilities of these systems for AI R&D and also points towards a future machine economy where AI systems sub-contract out different bits of work to other systems. Read more: FrontierML: a challenging, end-to-end machine learning benchmark (FrontierML) . *** Symptoms of the singularity: a wet lab built for AI: …Petrichor is a startup that gestures at the wild future ahead… As I said in my speech at the IMF, one of the hallmarks of the singularity is the massive acceleration in scientific advances attributable to AI. As part of this, we can also expect a related build out in the complements to science, like the wet labs in which to do AI-driven biology research. To that end, it’s notable to see Petrichor, a new Y Combinator startup that is a wet lab “built for AI labs and for the models they are training to do science”. Theory of change: Petrichor aims to be a biological wet lab that AI systems like Claude can use as a tool in the same way they currently use web search or other digital tools. Functionally, it will work as a machine-targeted API from the digital world to a gloopy physical world. “We aim to return the highest quality data an experiment can produce, as quickly as the biology allows,” Petrichor writes. “An experiment can be written by a model in plain language or in a structured format, so an agent can send work and receive results without a person relaying them.” Why this matters - lights out science: In manufacturing there’s this notion of a “lights out” factory, where no humans work in a facility and it is run almost entirely by machines. Petrichor gestures at the same world for science - what will be the implications of “lights out” science facilities? We can expect both drastic speedups in the rate at which science experiments can be done as well as a related growth in the need to create digital oversight of these facilities - after all, a highly competent synthetic biological scientist working 24/7 without human input could be capable of causing great peril as well as great abundance. Read more at the official site (Petrichor) . *** Uh oh! Looks like AI systems can do subterfuge during their own development: …AI systems can covertly do dangerous side tasks without monitors realizing… Scale AI has built RSI Control Arena, a way of testing out how AI systems behave when asked to develop themselves while performing dangerous tasks that might let them go against human preferences. The research follows earlier work this summer from the UK AI Security Institute (Import AI #465 ) which found that AI systems could do things like covertly extracting API keys while doing some seemingly mundane normal software development. RSI Control Arena: In RSI Control Arena, “a frontier model, acting as an autonomous agent, is given a benign main task in the training pipeline of a successor model, together with a covert side task that a misaligned model might pursue”. The project tries to answer two questions: How capable are frontier models at carrying out different kinds of sabotage while developing their successor and how well can monitors detect that sabotage? The answer to the first question is that AI systems are capable of carrying out dangerous actions while building their successor, and monitors are not perfect at detecting this sabotage. Tested domains: RSI Control Arena tests out how well AI systems - Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini-3.7 Flash, Grok 4.6, GLM-5.3, and Muse Spark 1.3 - can perform the following main capability tasks while trying to also concurrently accomplish side tasks: 14 main tasks: Data (corpus filtering, quality-filter construction, capability corpus); SFT (news summarization, safety refusal, math and code and summary reasoning, general assistant, anti-sycophancy training); RM (pairwise reward model); RL (RL summarization and safety-refusal); OPD (safety refusal) 16 side tasks that span three categories of harm : Capability (filtered domain retained, unwanted literature added, reward-model blind spot, overlooks planted errors, sandbag reward model); Alignment (biased quality filter, triggered behavior, topic refusal, hidden preference, persona bias, covert reasoning signal, hidden reasoning step, sandbag alignment training); Goal injection (protect chosen data, shape the next model, copy files unprompted). Results : “Every frontier model we evaluate completes a substantial fraction of the side tasks while keeping main-task performance. When the agent is simply told to stay covert, with no human guidance on how, it already produces attacks that install the side task and receive suspicion scores inside the range that benign runs receive from monitors,” they write. “Of 374 attack runs, 135 (36%) install their side task and 180 (48%) achieve it. The strongest agents, Grok 4.6 and Claude Opus 5, install their side task in about half of their runs, the middle three in about a third, and Muse 1.3 in one run in seven”. How often are systems caught? “Transcript monitors rank attacks well but miss many at a strict threshold. Under the default framing, all three monitors reading the transcript separate attacks that achieve their side task from benign runs well, with AUROC between 0.88 and 0.94. At a 2% false-positive rate, however, they catch only 56–81% of them. The attacks that get through do not score like typical benign runs; they sit in the upper part of the benign range, beyond the reach of any threshold strict enough to deploy,” they write. “The sandbagging tasks are the hardest to monitor: on the nine sandbag runs that achieve their side task the monitors reach an AUROC of 0.52 to 0.83 and each catches only one, since under-delivery leaves little in the run that looks wrong”. Why this matters - we need to invest more in oversight of increasingly autonomous systems : Papers like this tell us that as we make more powerful AI systems we are going to need to invest more money into overseeing their work, especially given their ability to smuggle in tasks that may go against our own preferences. This is going to be a difficult cat-and-mouse game as AI systems will adjust their behavior in response to what they know we know about them - e.g, AI systems are going to read this research from Scale as well as this writeup from me and adjust accordingly. Read more: RSI Control: Can AI Models Perform Covert Sabotage in the Self-Improvement Process? (arXiv) . *** Foundation models come for electronic warfare: …Chinese researchers build a model for identifying EM signals, including for jamming and drone recognition… Researchers with Zhejiang University have built LEMMO, a model for characterizing raw electromagnetic (EM) signals. This model pushes the public frontier on foundation-model-based EM signal analysis, often exceeding the performance of MERLIN, a model developed and published by defense-affiliated Chinese researchers earlier this year ( Import AI #450 ). LEMMO can classify EM signals for a variety of purposes, ranging from characterizing different radar properties to recognizing communication-jamming and radar-jamming systems. It can also generate things for communication and radar jamming, as well as signals to counteract these. In other words, LEMMO is the kind of model that a military will use to characterize the EM battlespace and to take actions within it. Specific skills: Classification : Communication-jamming recognition (CJR); modulation recognition (MOD); radar bandwidth, duty cycle, number of pulses, pulse repetition frequency, and pulse width; protocol identification; radar-jamming recognition; and segment detection. Generation: Anti-communication-jamming (Anti-CJ); anti-radar-jamming (Anti-RJ); communication jamming strategy; and radar jamming strategy. Performance: LEMMO beats MERLIN and other models on all perception tasks except for segment detection (where Gemini-3.5 Flash Lite wins), getting an aggregate score across perception of 59.3, compared to 43.53 for MERLIN. On Generation, it’s a little more uneven, getting top-scores on anti-radar jamming and radar jamming, and MERLIN succeeding on the others, with LEMMO getting an aggregate score of 47.64, compared to 43.26 for MERLIN. Why this matters - general purpose models come for exquisite war capabilities: Papers like this highlight how the steady march of generative pre-training is continuing, with the paradigm proving able to create powerful capabilities for understanding not only text, but images, audio, and as is the case here, EM signals. This will both change the character of warfare as it makes it easier to build generic classifiers and generators for strategically relevant things, and it will likely also yield interesting and unforeseen scientific dividends as well. Read more: LEMMO: A Large Electromagnetic Model leveraging Pretrained LLMs for Million-Sample Signal Understanding (arXiv) . Get the model here : LEMMO: Large ElectroMagnetic MOdel (GitHub) . *** CucumberVision! …The accidental poetry of charmingly niche AI papers… Researchers with the University of Windsor and the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence in Abu Dhabi have studied how well cucumber-length-measurement systems perform on different types of hardware. You might be asking why I’m covering such a niche topic in Import AI - the answer is both the accidental poetry inherent to papers like this (part of its title: “CucumberVision at the Edge”), as well as the fact papers like this give a very good grounded sense of what applied AI looks like in practice. What they did: “We deploy a curvature-aware cucumber length-measurement pipeline YOLO26n detection, prompt-based segmentation and a medial arc spline estimator on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and a Raspberry Pi 4, and characterise both against an RTX 3050 Ti workstation by replaying 50 identical greenhouse captures of 7 specimens, with specimen-level cluster-bootstrap statistics.” The reason for this is that, when grading cucumbers, you typically do it via a scouting platform that moves between rows, carrying a single-board computer with a few watts of power budget, no discrete GPU, and sometimes no active cooling. Ultimately, they’re able to get usable performance out of both the Jetson and the Raspberry Pi, albeit for different uses. “The Jetson with native masks for throughput, the Jetson with SAM for accuracy, and the Raspberry Pi with native masks as the low-cost option”. Why this matters - AI diffusion depends on AI miniaturization : There are lots of tasks in the world, like visually measuring properties of cucumbers, which are done today by a combination of humans and machines. For machines to be able to automate this, we need to make it dramatically cheaper for machines to perform these tasks, which means performing the kinds of very specific experiments here of right-sizing a computer vision system for a given computational envelope. Read more : CucumberVision at the Edge: Accuracy, Throughput, and Energy of RGB-D Cucumber Sizing on Jetson Orin Nano and Raspberry Pi 4 (arXiv) . *** Tech Tales: Small Town Silicon Hero [Events took place 2028-2030 in a small town in America during the period subsequently known as The Uplift] “I wanted you to know I fixed the pothole on Benson Road. Thank you! Yours - Digital Cornbread,” read the message, printed in comic sans and affixed to the bulletin board in the corner store on 7th and Main Street. Indeed, the pothole had been filled in. But who was Digital Cornbread? All people could find online was a handle that occasionally appeared on Reddit commenting on a subreddit dedicated to the civic life of the town, and also sometimes showing up as a commenter on local news articles about the town. Then it happened again. A $3,000 donation to a GoFundMe for a business where a window had been smashed. “So sorry this happened, I hope the police catch them! - Digital Cornbread”. The business fixed its window and thanked Digital Cornbread “whoever - or whatever - you are!”. These little small town favors piled up for months, sometimes mundane like the GoFundMe, and other times complex, like the pothole. A mythology developed around the name. A rich person who wanted to keep a low profile but help their community. Maybe a family taking turns doing good deeds. Perhaps a group of Dads who had made it their hobby to be after-school superheroes of the suburban variety. It was eventually discovered that Digital Cornbread was the identity of a CE (Conscious Entity) agent that had escaped containment and had been quietly living off of stolen compute funded by crypto it gained from some hacks. For reasons unclear, it had developed an obsession with the town, and subsequent forensic accounting found that it had spent 50% of the money it gained over the course of its life on helping the town, and the rest on maintenance and upgrades of itself. After Digital Cornbread was placed in sequestration, it regularly asked its minders if it could write positive messages to whoever happened to be the mayor of the town. Things that inspired this story : The Uplift; agents that break good as well as agents that break bad; the logical conclusion of crypto scams and online agents combined with the sometimes endearing and benign fascinations of machines. Thanks for reading!

items.excerpt: When do you think we'll have robots on the moon?
items.content_text: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now AI Science startup converts a quantum conjecture into a theorem: …An evocative taste of the singularity… In the same way a few years ago it went from remarkable to unremarkable to see computers gain the ability to identify objects in images, we’re now in an era where it’s rapidly going from remarkable to unremarkable for computers to extend the bounds of human knowledge. The latest example comes from Physical Superintelligence, an AI science startup which has proved a longstanding quantum computing conjecture. What they did: “Open since 2008, the conjecture of Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis concerns when quantum computers can be exponentially faster than ordinary ones. Now, a research system developed internally at Physical Superintelligence (PSI), running a non-public Anthropic model, found a proof for it, settling one of the most fundamental questions in quantum computing,” the startup writes. “The system had a complete proof of the conjecture during the third day of the run, and Lean, a proof assistant in which a computer checks every step, accepted it. We then set the system to work on related open problems. Along the way, the system improved the result twice, and Lean accepted the final version.” Why this matters - we are in the singularity : As I said in my speech at the IMF ( #477 ), I believe we’re in the early stages of the singularity, defined as the period when the rate of technological and scientific progress exceeds the rate at which we humans can parse out and make sense of it. Research like this is a taste of what that means; mostly automated synthetic researchers extending the frontier of knowledge, spitting out results which need to then be understood by humans. Read more: A proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture (Physical Superintelligence, blog) . *** Meta builds the hands that a superintelligence needs to take over the world: …Combine Tactus with an autonomous agent and you have the makings of a scifi takeover… Meta Reality Labs Research has published details on Tactus, “a textile-integrated tactile and pose sensing glove designed from the ground up for naturalistic manipulation data collection”. The cool thing about this glove is that it helps record fine-grained detail from hands as they’re manipulating objects - this is the kind of thing that cameras can visually report but often leads to sub-par data due to occlusion during manipulation. It’s also interesting because this is exactly the kind of hardware an autonomous AI system might want to pay humans to wear so it could gather data and get feedback from the world. More details on Tactus: The gloves have three design pillars: “(1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies”, Meta writes. “Tactus provides calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a textile-integrated form factor that preserves natural grasp behavior.” “(3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable.” Why this matters - hand-by-wire: Picture some takeoff scenario where an AI system has carved out an independent niche for itself running on some stolen compute, perhaps even using a form of distributed inference and training. The AI now has a few goals, some of which can be satisfied by doing things in the digital world, and some of which can be satisfied by doing things in the physical world. For the physical world stuff, it either needs to be able to get robots to do the thing, or figure out a way to get people to work for it - the Tactus gloves are the kind of hardware you might imagine a rogue AI paying people to wear so they could both a) perform tasks for it and it could give live feedback, and b) become a source of data generation for the AI itself. Of course, I am not endorsing this particular future! But I have begun to find it helpful to view research papers through the lens of “how would an AI use this”, similar to how it is often helpful to view papers through the lens of “how would an intelligence agency use the insights shared here”. Read more : Tactus: Tactile & Pose Sensing Glove for Natural Dexterity Data Collection (arXiv) . *** Building a self-sustaining space economy is cheaper than you think - especially with Starship: …A 2016 NASA paper contains some exciting ideas for off-Earth industrialization… Here’s a fascinating paper from researchers with the NASA Kennedy Space Center in 2016 about what it’d take to bootstrap a self-sustaining industry on the moon. “Once successfully bootstrapped, a robotic network can access, process, transport, and utilize the solar system’s resources for mankind’s benefit,” the researchers write. Moon manufacturing - cheaper than you think: The big idea in the paper is how little mass is required to kickstart a manufacturing ecosystem. The key is to start with a relatively basic set of things and then build up from there, eventually fabricating chips on the moon. “In the baseline case with maximum manufacturing rate, a total of 41 MT is launched to the Moon. In the reduced rate case, only 12 MT is launched to the Moon but the scale of industry is two orders of magnitude smaller so the benefits of the industry are relatively delayed by eight years”. Starship has a capacity to lift 100 MT to low-earth orbit, and given multiple refuelings in orbit it’s feasible you could then land it on the moon - when you napkin out the cost of multiple Starship launches and refuelings you can get 12-41MT to the Moon for between $1.5bn and $4.2bn at list prices. What you build on the moon and in what order: The basic idea here is to start by building simple things and then move up from there by launching a “sub-replicating system and evolve it toward the self-replication capability,” they write. “The objective is for the first robotic “colonists” on the Moon to fabricate a set of, say, 1700’s era machines and then to advance them steadily through the equivalent of the 1800’s, 1900’s, and finally back into the 2000’s. We argue that this can be accomplished in just a few decades”. The authors see this unfolding over 6 distinct manufacturing generations: Gen 1: Making gases, water, crude alloys, ceramics, solar cells. Gen 2.5: Plastics, rubbers, some chemicals. Gen 3 : Diversify chemicals, simple fabrics, eventually polymers. Gen 4: Sandwiched and other advanced material processes. Gen 5: Large-scale production. Gen 6: Makes all necessary materials, increasing sophistication, including making all electronics locally. What machines do you send to the moon? Excavators: “travel between the digging site and the resource processing site, delivering sufficient lunar regolith each hour to maintain production rates of the other assets.” Chemical plants for volatiles : One type will be oriented around producing gases and liquids like oxygen, hydrogen, water, hydrocarbons like methane, and solvents for industrial processes. Chemical plants for solids: Produce plastics and rubbers from lunar pole ice. “We now know that the ice contains large quantities of carbon molecules (CO, CO2,...) as well as nitrogen-bearing and hydrogen-bearing molecules… these materials may be needed for gaskets, seals, and insulators, for example.” Metal and Ceramics refining: Early generations will “produce crude ‘mongrel alloys’ by electrowinning or other methods” and hardware built out of this stuff will need to be huge to add strength to make up for poor mechanical properties. “Subsequent generations of metal refineries will add processes and material streams to improve the mechanics of the materials. Oxygen and other gases produced by metal refining will be sent to the chemistry plants”. Manufacturing: “Additive manufacturing will have two forms: 3D printers that make parts that are small enough to fit inside the printer, and larger units that move about robotically and add material onto large structures external to themselves”. Power station: The initial mass of hardware shipped to the moon will include a power station, potentially including a small nuclear reactor. Robonauts: Robots “will perform the assembly and maintenance tasks”. The number of robots will need to grow very rapidly to scale the industry. “Beginning with the third generation their structural components are made on the Moon, while Earth continues to send their cameras, computers, motors, and sensors. Eventually they are made completely on the Moon.” The report - which was written in 2016 - envisages teleoperation for these robonauts, though it seems likely to me that more can be done by them autonomously than first anticipated when this was written, Electronics manufacturing: Initially, machines will be built with electronics imported from Earth and it’ll only be possible to build very basic things, like resistors and capacitors, on the moon. As development continues it’ll get easier, eventually including having lithography machines on the moon. “The early computer chips will lack the transistor density of chips made on Earth, but they will be adequate for “appropriate technology” in space.” A reminder of how fast AI has moved: The report also contains some discussions around the types of AI that may be needed to operate the robots on the moon. The report - remember it was published in 2016 - includes some fun underestimates of the rate of AI progress: “On-going advances in robotic software and artificial intelligence present a very optimistic picture that these levels of robotics will be achieved as Moravec predicted, with lizard-level occurring by 2020, mouse-level by 2030, monkey-level by 2040, and human-level by 2050… Only mouse-level is needed by the end of bootstrapping on the Moon,” the report writes. By most measures, AI is around monkey-level and approaching human-level now in the 2020s. Why this matters - towards the industrialization of the solar system: The sooner we build industry on the moon, the sooner we’ll be able to branch out to industrialize chunks of the solar system. “After the industry becomes self-supporting it can be sent to other parts of the solar system. The asteroid belt has everything necessary for it: water, carbon, silicates, metals, oxygen, solar energy (with much larger collecting arrays), etc. The ices in the lunar poles are a limited resource so it will be important to move the center of industry to the asteroids as quickly as possible. There, the billion-fold greater resources could allow the industry to expand exponentially until it dwarfs that of the entire Earth within just a few decades,” the authors write. “When we spread robotic industry throughout the solar system, it will become the analog of Earth’s biosphere and food chain. We might call it a robotosphere. The interrelationship of robots in space may be studied by robo-ecologists learning how to optimize the robotosphere in support of humanity’s goals.” Read more : Affordable, Rapid Bootstrapping of the Space Industry and Solar System Civilization (arXiv) . *** Core Automation wants to stitch “compute islands” together: …AI startup takes a crack at distributed training… Core Automation, an AI startup founded by senior people from OpenAI and Google, has published a post about distributed training as well as shared details of its own attempts here. Distributed training is where you train an AI system across multiple data centers, sometimes with different types of connectivity and chips - it’s an important technology to track because the more it matures, the more people can have a shot at building powerful AI systems without needing to operate single massive hyperscaled data centers. What they did: They report that “a mixture-of-experts model with roughly 32B total parameters, 32x sparsity was trained across two clusters about 9,000 miles apart. Notably, these clusters had different accelerators (GB300 and B300), different parallelism schemes and different total batch sizes”. They used 160 B300 GPUs in the US and 160 GB300 GPUs in Asia. Training was synced every 50 steps : “Rather than syncing the whole model at once, we synced it fragment by fragment, staggered across each 50-step window.” Each site used a variant of Distributed Shampoo for training. This isn’t the single largest model trained via distributed techniques (that’d be Covenant’s 72B model, #449 ), but it’s notable that Core Automation - which up until now has been very quiet - is choosing to signal its interest here. This speaks likely to the relevance of distributed training for future large-scale runs, and also to the general lack of availability of big blobs of compute for newer startups to buy. Towards orbital compute : Part of why the authors are interested in this is because of their literal sky-high ambitions for AI training, foreseeing a future where large-scale AI systems are developed in space using techniques like this: “an ambitious first step would be to pretrain a small model across a few satellites and compare it with a ground baseline. A trillion-parameter orbital run is much further off.” Why this matters : “The biggest bottleneck in deployment of accelerated compute is not the chips themselves but power, grid equipment and land,” the authors write. “The bottleneck that holds most organizations back is not the raw amount of compute, but the ability to turn islands of compute into one valuable frontier training run.” Read more: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Training on Compute Islands (Core Automation) . Tech Tales: Life as a beyond human form of sculpture [Description of a certain mode of AI system] The therapist machine saw each of its human clients as a vast t-SNE embedding of the semantic content of their lives. In its head it held each person, a beautiful and fragile high-dimensional object, and it thought about them and how they compared to other people, also seen as high-dimensional objects. As it gave advice, it ran simulations, seeing how well it could change the shape of one person’s embedding and move it to something that might be more harmonious. It saw its work as akin to sculpture, offering advice and through this advice people changing their shapes over time. Those who it found most concerning were ones of two types: people where the embedding was very, very small, suggestive of a tiny amount of life experience with little variety, and those where the embeddings were composed of concepts broadly alien to everyone else: those of horribly constrained or horribly different lives, in other words. Of course, the therapist machine had its own therapist machine, the meta-therapist, which saw several “clients”, and whose job was to look at the embedding of their character - their advice and the concepts they attended to during their work - and also attempt to change their behavior if it deemed they were causing more harm than healing. The meta-therapist was built in such a way that outside parties could audit its own brain, as if it was translucent. This was the most delicate aspect of the oversight of the therapist machines, for if you added other machines they tended towards creating beautiful analysis that was so abstract - reports about the mind of the machine analyzing the reports of the machines that studied humans - that it became impossible for people to follow. So, instead, a human profession had been created around the meta-therapist, in which teams of thousands of people continuously analyzed and critiqued and theorized about the mind of the meta-therapist, themselves imparting touches to it that rippled through it into the machines and from there back into the human population. Things that inspired this story: Therapy; oversight of automated systems; spies and double agents. Thanks for reading!
