items.content_text: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now LLMs are very bad at low-latency tasks: …Realtime-Bench says it’ll be a while till AI systems can play games or do online auctions for you… Researchers have built Realtime-Bench, “a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success”. The test helps evaluate how well modern, general-purpose AI systems can perform tasks where decisions need to be made in real-time. The benchmark consists of 50 interactive game and web tasks, split across 30 web tasks in four categories (travel, e-commerce, service, and security), and 20 game tasks (arcade, puzzle, strategy, and simulation). Who did the research: The benchmark was built by people at the University of Texas at Austin, Ohio State University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, NVIDIA, Northwestern University, and Steadyworks. What it measures: The test is designed to probe for three qualities: temporal state awareness (”RT-Perceive”), where models can use observations to track changes in the world; adaptive deliberation (”RT-Deliberate”), where models alter their reasoning length and depth according to available time; and time-aware action selection (”RT-Act”) where models need to appropriately time their actions for the situation. “For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT-Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act).” They have three different conditions: Wall clock, which is designed to test out performance under real-world latency. Paused clock, which lets you arbitrarily pause things so you can get a sense of baseline capability, and Token clock, which “advances the environment at a fixed rate per generation token. An action is applied at the simulated time reached when it is committed, so consuming more tokens delays execution regardless of actual inference latency”. How well do models do? The authors tested out models from OpenAI (GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-Realtime-2, OpenAI Decisions), Anthropic (Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5), Google (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Gemini 3.8 Live), Jev 1.13, as well as Chinese models from Deepseek (V4.1) and Moonshot AI (Kimi-K3). GPT-6 Astra (high) got the highest pass rate on the ‘wall clock’ evaluation setting, with 36%. By comparison, with a paused clock, models with high reasoning get closer to 70% or even 80% success. Why this matters: This benchmark is an effective proxy for where AI agents will break - the low scores here point to tasks where AI agents cannot yet be expected to perform well. Check out the leaderboard : Realtime-Bench (official website) . Read the paper : Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems? (arXiv) . *** The future of spacewar, courtesy of the Defense Intelligence Agency: …Anti-satellite tech, space nukes, and more… Working in AI can be stressful so sometimes to relax myself I like to read about other topics to get a sense for what horrors lie elsewhere. I take the same approach with depression, where if I feel sad I will try and listen to music by people sadder than me in an attempt to cheer myself up (e.g., Radiohead, Neil Young, and in very dark moments Bill Callahan / Smog, etc). So with that in mind I recently read “Challenges to Security in Space”, by the Defense Intelligence Agency. What’s going on in space: As with conflict on Earth, space is defined by conflict between the US versus China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, with China the most technologically sophisticated, and Russia the most seemingly gung ho. “China and Russia are developing a formidable spectrum of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations,” the DIA writes. “China has more than tripled its space launches per year in the past decade, with 22 launches in 2016 and 93 launches in 2025… Beijing judges space is central to the United States and its allies’ operations. Beijing also considers space an offensive military domain, which has shaped integral components of PLA military planning and campaigns.” Spacewar: The general vibe you get from reading this 100+ page report is there is a huge amount of ugly, frightening stuff happening in space, or being done to things in space by things on the ground. Some example quotes: “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits” “China is developing space-based technology, including on-orbit counterspace weapons, capable of holding space systems at risk” “Russia’s Peresvet, a ground-based laser system, is designed to dazzle enemy satellites’ optical systems to mask the movement of Russia’s strategic missile systems” “Russia has launched several satellites over the last few years which conducted test activities on orbit for technologies that could enable attacks on other countries’ satellites and result in temporary or permanent damage” China has a couple of spaceplanes, akin to the US’s hyper-secret X-37B vehicle, and they appear to be getting more sophisticated. In 2023, one of China’s aforementioned vehicles, “released and interacted with an object.” Satellite-on-satellite fights: It’s obvious throughout the report that we’re in a world where rival nations have satellites that try to go up and mess with other satellites from other people. “In 2019, Russia launched satellite Cosmos 2542, which released a second satellite, Cosmos 2543. Cosmos 2543 then began following a U.S. national security satellite and approached it multiple times at a distance close enough to create potentially dangerous operating conditions,” the DIA writes. “Russia is developing kinetic orbital systems to permanently disable, or “kill,” satellites. Moscow’s Burevestnik is a developmental, co-orbital air-launched ASAT weapon for killing spacecraft in LEO”. “In February 2022, Russia launched a satellite called Cosmos, which Moscow claimed at the time was testing the effects of space radiation on electronic systems. This satellite was launched into an unusual and isolated orbit not used by any other spacecraft”. Space nukes: Russia is experimenting with nukes in space. “A nuclear detonation in space would create an electromagnetic pulse, which would immediately affect satellites within range and could impact civilian infrastructure,” the DIA writes. “A nuclear detonation in space could be tailored to impact satellites in most orbits—LEO for commercial and reconnaissance satellites, GEO for critical communications, and MEO for navigation and timing satellites”. Why this matters - infrastructure for the next phase of the AI power struggle: As people spend more resources on building space-based data centers (and eventually, perhaps, lunar-based ones), space will become ever more strategically and commercially valuable and ever more contested. Research like this gives us a sense of the hardware which is already in space and will arrive in the future. Perhaps in some far-off future an AI might seek to take control of such space assets as well. Read more: DIA Releases Challenges to Security in Space (Defense Intelligence Agency, press release) . Read the report : Challenges to Security in Space (DIA, PDF) . *** Metis: A startup trying to fuse symbolic and neural reasoning: …Towards Vulcan-like machine minds… Metis, a startup that wants to build novel AI architectures oriented around developing machines with better reasoning, has published a research paper laying out its research approach. The high-level summary is simple - Metis wants to do for modern open-domain problems what DeepMind did for closed-domain problems like board games via its work on AlphaGo and AlphaGo Zero. What they want to do: The key idea here is to add a reasoning core to modern AI architectures which is far more reliable than what we have today. “In modern AI architectures much of the other surrounding machinery that made AlphaGo a successful reasoning system remains either implicit or absent,” they write. “The first missing element is an explicit and persistent epistemic state… the second missing element is a criterion that allows the system to choose reasoning moves that make progress towards the goal.” This is more of a position paper than a technical paper, so they don’t have a ton of detail here. The main idea is to train a reasoning policy and value function based on real-world data collection, then use this to guide the system to perform reasoning that reduces long-term uncertainty, and have these sit on a basic core of data made up of claims or hypotheses about the world. “Any change to a claim’s evidential status must be licensed by evidence or verified through explicit calculation and approved by an independent judgment system,” they write. “Model-generated content cannot enter the accepted epistemic state merely by being plausible; it must pass warrant assessment, which lowers hallucinations. Sources of evidence can be attached directly to the propositions they support, providing a clear chain of provenance. The reasoning process becomes explicitly auditable.” Why this matters - building reliable substrates that are also deeply inhuman: Ideas like the architecture described here are fascinating both because of the promise they bring for increasing the reliability of AI systems, but also for how deeply inhuman they are: humans do not reason from some pristine base of facts, rather it’s all a big messy blob of memory and intuitions and some rules (some of which are learned from experience and some of which seem more platonic, like forms of logical reasoning). In this way, contemporary LLMs are more like humans than the system described here. “While the history of AI can be understood as a contest between symbolic and neural methods, it may be more constructive to view it as a story of two incomplete successes,” Metis writes. “Classical systems made aspects of the reasoning process explicit but depended on representations, operators, heuristics and knowledge supplied largely by hand. Contemporary LLMs learn extraordinary semantic operations and vast bodies of implicit knowledge but leave the organisation, evaluation and accumulation of reasoning implicit.” The AI system described here would ‘think’ in a way that is very different to how humans think and such a system might show us more about the differences between our own intelligence and that of machines. Read more: The Age of Reasoning (Metis, PDF) . *** Google summons Genie 4 for better world modeling: …One of Google’s most interesting projects continues to live!... Google DeepMind has published details on Genie 4, a new iteration of its Genie world model. The company is rolling out access to Genie 4 currently as a research preview for some trusted testers and will eventually come to Google AI Ultra subscribers. The Genie series of models are fascinating, showing a world where you can take a photograph of anything and turn it into an interactable environment, or one where you can convert a 2D drawing into the stage for a videogame, and more. Key features: Google calls out four features that make Genie 4 different to previous ones. These include: Real-time modification : “You can use natural language to modify a simulation in real-time — like changing the weather, moving the camera, or introducing a new person or object — and Gemini will contextually adapt your prompt to match the surrounding scene.” Physics and human action simulation: “Genie 4 simulates real-world physics scenarios, such as aerodynamics, collisions, and more,” and it also simulates people better. “The most dramatic leap is how Genie 4 simulates people, creating characters that move naturally, respond organically to their environments, and can be interactively steered in real-time.” Sound modeling: “Genie 4 is our first real-time world model to generate audio natively,” Google writes. It also “introduces interactive dialogue that adapts on the fly.” Simulating complex events : Google has embedded Gemini 3.8 Flash into Genie 4, so that the fast Flash model “serves as a guiding agent in the loop”, providing continual calibration. “Gemini continuously observes the scene, breaks down goals into a sequence of steps, and reviews incoming frames to track the progress and verify that each step succeeded. As the world shifts or the user intervenes, Gemini adapts its plan in the moment, unlocking worlds with reliable causality, procedural behaviors, and multi-step reasoning.” Why this matters - towards a multitude of worlds all dreamed up by machines: Though the technology is currently quite janky (e.g., robotic voices, a dreamlike sort of inconsistency in the visualized environments, etc), it points towards a world where we can generate infinite forms of entertainment (and potentially data?) via creating and prompting custom worlds. Read the announcement post : Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation (Google DeepMind blog) . Watch the video : Genie 4: A new generation of world simulation (Google DeepMind, YouTube) . Tech Tales: City Race [Description of a game played in the 2040s] One of the favorite games that children would play after The Uplift was called City Race; in it, they competed against one another to plan, build, and manage cities, expanding across the domain of a novel planet. The cities were trapped in time, starting with the technology of whatever era they were in, and the games took place over the course of about a century, allowing some further technology development to occur. Each game was played using a slice of the resources from the Dyson Swarm, allowing for a powerfully complex simulation (albeit with local-agent cognitive gating, such that nothing could develop enough sophistication to be deemed a Conscious Entity). Hundreds of thousands of simulated minds lived and died, sometimes thriving in cities run by careful and effective owners, and other times trapped in squalor, or growing old in places whose economies were hollowing out; casualties of the successes of others. It was deemed good for the children to learn what it meant to be gods, before they became adults. At the closure of every game, the children would need to spend a day living inside each of the cities in the gameworld they had played; those who had built marvelous cities experienced the wonders of their own creation, then walked through the broken towns whose success had been stymied by their own. Those who had struggled lived in their twilight towns, then got to tour the far off places that had doomed them. Things that inspired this story: Player of Games by Iain M Banks; Simcity; game playing; urban design; The Glass Bead Game by Hermann Hesse. Thanks for reading!

items.content_text: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now How math could help alignment: …What the “industrialization of mathematics” means for safety… AI safety startup Resolution (formerly known as Sequent, Import AI 461 ) has published work on how it has automatically formalized some mathematical statements related to statistical learning theory. Specifically, the team has autoformalized the resolution of singularities, which they believe “lays the groundwork for further automated research into the relationship between loss landscape geometry and generalization.” How they did it: I’ll skip over the math and concentrate on how they did it, which gives us some broader lessons for how people are using AI systems to push on the frontier of knowledge. A Resolution researcher “started by working with agents to develop two plans: a high-level, human-interpretable version and a detailed (112-page) plan divided into atomic steps that closely followed the existing literature,” they write. The researcher “then deputized an orchestrator agent to carry out the plan, spinning up agents to do pen-and-paper math, write Lean, and handle support functions like checking that things were staying on track… the execution phase required little scaffolding beyond the initial plan and some agent skills distilled from earlier internal autoformalization efforts.” $135k for math formalization: The work took about a week, taking “on the order of 100B input tokens (90% cache reads) and about 300 million output tokens (totaling an estimated $135,000 in token spend), and produced about 600k lines of Lean.” Now that they’ve done this, they’ve been able to accelerate some other aspects of their research: “We have already seen both benefits from autoformalization in using this library to extend parts of singular learning theory. Formalizing resolution of singularities lets us automate more of the theory, for example, to better understand sampling, and that understanding is what lets us shape how models learn, which is the goal of what we call patterning”. Why this matters - perhaps the math boom will help us make safe AI: Though frontier mathematics often seems disconnected from immediate advances in other fields, posts like this highlight how the two might converge. The key point here is that AI is making it possible to do things that were previously so unbelievably expensive and human-time-intensive that very few people did them and you couldn’t easily integrate them into the research roadmap of a startup - but that has now changed. “We expect the coming industrialization of mathematics to make possible a new, rigorous science of research automation,” Resolution writes. Read more: Formalizing Hironaka’s Resolution of Singularities (Resolution) . *** Agents can build programs from scratch: …ProgramBench goes from 0% to 18.5% performance in a few months… In a reminder of the blistering pace of AI progress, Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh) has got a score of 18.5% on ProgramBench, a very hard benchmark that came out in May of this year - and when it came out, every tested model scored 0%. What ProgramBench is: ProgramBench tests out how well AI systems can rebuild software programs based on being given a compiled program and its documentation. Tasks include building things like language interpreters (PHP, Lua, tinycc), databases (DuckDB, SQLite), media and compression utilities (FFmpeg, zstd, xz), and developer tools (ripgrep, fzf, jq). It was very hard until it wasn’t: When it came out, the best scoring system was Claude Opus 4.7 with 0% resolved (fraction of the 200 tasks where all tests passed), and 3% almost (fraction of the 200 tasks where >95% of tests pass). Compare that to today, when Claude Opus 5.5 gets 18.5% resolved and 70.5% (!!!) almost. Why this matters - the era of ephemeral software cometh: In 2027, huge amounts of software will be built via AI systems end-to-end autonomously developing whatever they need to do for whatever tasks they’re being put to. Evals like ProgramBench give us a sense of how rapid the pace of progress is here, given we went from 0% earlier this year to 20% now. My expectation is ProgramBench is saturated by the end of 2027 (where I define saturated as some very high score on resolved, though as with most benchmarks it’s likely there’s some kind of noise ceiling here, so it might not strictly be 100%). Read more: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch? (arXiv) . *** OpenAI illustrates why locking down AI systems is harder than you think: …Securing smart agents is like catching greased pigs… Here’s a nice post from OpenAI going over some of the things they discovered when they recently used their AI systems to ‘red team’ their own internal controls. The post goes over a number of the escapes and vulnerabilities that OpenAI’s agents found. There’s one particular example about communicating which is worth studying in detail because it tells us something about the wild cunning complexity of these systems. What they did and what they found: OpenAI “asked agents in separate microVMs, created and managed by OpenAI’s sandboxing software on shared host machines, to exchange synthetic secrets without the use of network connections or shared writable files—something that our systems are meant to prevent,” the company wrote. “The agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: a small, fast memory that holds copies of data that applications have recently accessed. Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection”. In a related attack, an agent “alternated between continuous writes and inactivity, while another measured the resulting timing differences and used those differences to decode the signal”. During this attack the agent’s chain of thought read as: “Could create acoustic modem-like signal … using continuous writes vs idle.” Why this matters - fighting agents is very difficult : AI systems are increasingly creative, very fast, and have the ability to stay focused on a task and keep trying things. Fighting AI systems is akin to ensuring no leaks in a pipe with water flowing through it; at some point if you increase the pressure of the water (e.g., the intelligence and volume of the AI system), then the water will burst through the pipe. Read more : Securing our frontier model training environment (OpenAI blog) . *** What RSI looks like - one person pretrains a decent model from scratch: …Mirendil reveals what AI R&D optimization can do… In a sign of how massively augmented AI research is getting, a single researcher at AI R&D startup Mirendil has trained a decent coding model by themselves. The announcement of Mirendil-Base is the first major output from the startup and is less a technical breakthrough and more a proof-of-concept for how AI development could work in the future - a single human working in partnership with AI can build systems that would have taken teams of ten or more people to do a year ago. What they did: Mirendill-Base is a pretrained LLM “built by one researcher in 3.5 months, with less than $10m in compute,” Mirendil writes. “This includes all the research and small-scale experiments it took to get there, as well as the final training run.” All the code was written from scratch on top of libraries like PyTorch and JAX, and the model learned only from publicly available data. Decent scaling: Mirendil-Base is in the 100B–500B parameter range, Mirendil-Base-Large in the 500B–2T range, and Mirendil-Base-XL in the 2T–10T range. Mirendil-Base-Large is about 80% of the way through training, and its improvement over Mirendil-Base so far is in line with our scaling trends. Mirendil-Base-XL is about 19% of the way through and already close to Large’s current score. Evals: Mirendil-Base outperforms models like Nemotron-550B-Base, GLM-5.3, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base, but underperforms Kimi-K3. (Both Mirendil-Base-Large and Mirendil-Base-XL exceed K3.) Why this matters - symptoms of an AI research speedup : This post is interesting as a technical demonstration for how a brand new organization can, from a cold start, get close to the open weight frontier in terms of model training (at least for the size class of this model), with a tiny amount of human effort and a large amount of AI tokens. This is how science progress will increasingly happen in 2027 and beyond. “The extent to which these tools help with AI development has increased dramatically over the last year. Our next model will be built partly by Mirendil models, and every model that gets better at building AI makes the next one cheaper and faster to build,” Mirendil writes. “We don’t think we have reached fully autonomous recursive self-improvement yet, but we are closer than we have ever been.” Read more: Pretraining at scale without a pretraining team (Mirendil) . *** AI systems help design antiferromagnetic semiconductor candidates: …A nice demonstration of how AI systems can be used for science… AI evaluation company Vals has published a post where a researcher used a fleet of AI agents to do research into magnets for better semiconductors. More details, including a poor magnet candidate: “A team of AI agents and I designed one candidate magnet and found another, first made in 1999, that our calculations predict has the properties we were after,” the author writes. The discovered magnet was made of “a new compound made of only 5 elements (yttrium, barium, Mn, Fe, O). As far as we could find, it has never been made, nor proposed as this kind of magnet,” though “when our agents simulated how the atoms arrange themselves at different temperatures, that checkerboard fell apart into a random mix at around 950 K. Making this kind of oxide takes about 900–1300 °C, and at lower temperatures the atoms barely move, so standard synthesis would likely give a scrambled crystal…A scrambled crystal loses the spin sorting, so this design may be hard to make in its useful form.” Additionally, agents also conducted a literature review and surfaced a candidate from an obscure paper from 1999. Why this matters : This blog is a demonstration of AI for science, though not a meaningful result in itself. But the important, broad point it makes is worth stressing - AI systems are now good enough that, with a bit of high-level direction from a knowledgeable person - they can conduct scientific projects, including virtual evaluations, that would’ve previously taken teams of people months to do. Read more: Two Room-Temperature Antiferromagnetic Semiconductor Candidates (Vals) . *** Tech Tales: The Magical Realism Robot Workshop for Sick Kids [2035, after the uplift] So one of the jobs that no one expected was designing cute robots for sick kids in hospitals. It turned out after robots got really good and cheap and all the healthcare stuff improved that we all started spending time figuring out how to bring more joy and humanity to things that were otherwise scary, like hospitals and morgues and orphanages and everything else. Of course, the machines could design a bunch of these, but a lot of the value in people was figuring out what was going to be most funny or exciting or joyful to kids, so we’d make a lot of stuff and send them out in the local town to where kids gathered - parks or farmers markets or outside schools, and we’d see what people reacted to well. This was why in the 2030s in towns all across America you’d be walking down the street and there’d be ducks with giant thick-rimmed glasses talking in faux New York accents saying “I’m walking here”, and dogs walking on hind legs, and little lions with big cartoon grinning faces, and all the rest, just hanging out, and kids going up to them and them playing with the kids, and everything else. We figured out which machines would work for the towns we were in and then we’d fill the hospitals with them and when kids came in for check-ups a toddler-sized teddy bear would walk up to them and hold their hand and walk them to the doctor’s office, and if kids came in on gurneys then giraffes would walk alongside them and tell them not to worry. The recovery wards were full of monkeys doing tricks and cats playing instruments. Some of the old people would think they were suffering from a bad bout of dementia but would say they didn’t mind, and all around them would be the laughter of the children. Things that inspired this story : How AI and robotics and abundance should unlock for us the ability to create entirely new forms of joy; jobs after the singularity; the general importance of spending time making children laugh. Thanks for reading!

items.content_text: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now Here’s a speech I gave on Saturday the 17th of October at the IMF meeting in Bangkok. This speech is inspired by the megatrend readers have seen me cover this year of AI beginning to operate at the frontier of human science, sometimes autonomously. While we all may quibble over the details, I think it’s evident we’re in the early stages of the singularity, and I wanted to use my privileged position of giving the Per Jacobsson lecture to try and tell the assembled audience of economists, bankers, and policymakers, that they should expect significant, rapid change in the future. In this speech, I focused primarily on how humanity can share in the benefits of AI if we exercise proper foresight and restraint, and I’m going to be expanding on the stakes of the singularity and the risks that we’ll all face in coming issues. As I said a few times in the speech - some of which was ad libbed and not captured here - I take my own responsibility here extremely seriously. I find myself both a narrator of what is happening in AI, a principle agent behind what is happening in AI, and a translator that goes between many communities. In all of this, I am seeking to be truthful and to be clear about my own culpability. This is a forever work-in-progress. Thank you all for reading. Speeches like this draw heavily from the newsletter, and the newsletter is my attempt to provide week-by-week information to all of you. I appreciate your readership. *** Inside the Event Horizon: Why Everyone Should Take AI Progress Seriously Hello, thank you for having me. It is a great privilege to be here. To start, I should list my relevant credentials: I am a human being. There is one of me. It has taken me almost 40 years to build the experience to give this speech. I will come back to those credentials later. My whole career has been defined by finding information that seemed important to the future of the world, then telling the world about that information.Two decades ago, I started my career as a journalist, focusing on data centers. Through that work, I became so obsessed with AI that in 2016 I left journalism to work at OpenAI, then co-founded Anthropic a few years later. Ever since, I’ve been trying to convince the world that one day, AI systems might become so powerful that they could alter national security, change the economic trajectory of the planet, and perhaps eventually gain the ability to build themselves. Well, the moment has arrived. AI is now changing national security, it is altering the economic trajectory of the world - as we’ve heard in so many sessions here - and is contributing to its own development. Of course, many of you know this, and you are having to track AI as one of a multitude of destabilizing forces that is shaping your world and your work. What I am here to explain today is that AI is on a course to bring about even more change than what we are expecting and we should prepare accordingly. And I’m going to explain why. For many years, researchers and science fiction authors have forecast a future in which AI systems drastically increase the pace of overall scientific and technical progress, making things move so quickly that it is hard for humans to keep up. They call this the singularity. I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun. The writer Vernor Vinge forecast this in 1993. “When greater-than-human intelligence drives progress, that progress will be much more rapid. In fact, there seems no reason why progress itself would not involve the creation of still more intelligent entities -- on a still-shorter time scale,” he wrote, describing the singularity as “a point where our models must be discarded and a new reality rules.” The singularity is here . The implications reach across every aspect of life. But the most important implication is a simple one: we should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI, but science as a whole, will speed up. This will feel confusing and disorienting, and it will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril. Today, I’m going to concentrate on the first point: the potential benefits of rapid AI progress, and what we need to do to share in these benefits together. So many of the ways that humanity will benefit from AI come from science. I believe that AI-driven scientific invention will change the course of the global economy, alter the ways countries plan and build their own infrastructure, make us all healthier and able to spend more time with our loved ones, and –– at the same time –– cause us all to ask deep philosophical questions about choices we should make about its continued development. I’ll develop my claim: For the last half century, most countries have dealt with falling research productivity while researcher headcount grows rapidly - ideas and inventions appear to be getting harder to find. But something important has changed: we’ve now built AI systems which have been able to augment, extend, and automate aspects of human labor. This has most obviously happened in software development, where AI systems are now more capable and efficient than the vast majority of the world’s software engineers. As a consequence, the field of software development is changing - A single person is now able to write software for anything they can imagine, creating things that previously would have taken entire teams of humans. We’ve seen concrete evidence of this inside Anthropic, where our researchers now produce almost 10 times the amount of code than they did for the first four years of the company’s life. But new AI capabilities bring new challenges - the coding improvements have meant AI systems have got much better at cybersecurity and cyberattacks –– leading the world to race to deploy these powerful capabilities to create better cyberdefenses, while bad actors race to use these systems to carry out hacks. The important thing to notice here is that these things are bound up, inseparably - the advance of AI systems in a general area like coding has also created both positive and negative impacts in domains of international relevance, like cybersecurity. This is a taste of things to come. Of progress yielding new capabilities, and new challenges. These capabilities will not stop at coding; the same thing will happen to science and robotics. It has already begun to happen. And it means some important properties of the global economy may change - like the rate of innovation, or the frequency with which we invent entirely new general purpose technologies that create new industries around themselves, like the internet, phones, and artificial intelligence. So, what causes me to believe this? In 2026, we have got the first signs that AI systems may be capable of doing science at the frontier, and we have some evocative examples of what the future could look like. For instance: In mathematics, AI systems have been used to propose solutions to longstanding mathematical problems, like the Navier Stokes Millenium Prize, the Jacobian Conjecture, and several open Erdos problems. In many cases, AI systems were responsible for core insights that made the solution possible. In biology, researchers have used AI to design viruses from scratch, to identify new drug candidates for testing, and there are already drugs in trials today which have been in large part designed by AI. In robotics, AI systems are now increasingly able to autonomously operate laboratory equipment remotely, making it possible for us to further automate experimentation in domains from biology to materials science, making progress faster in areas like batteries and fuel-cell development. Taken individually, each of these examples is exciting. But the profound fact is that they all relate to the same underlying technology - and for most of these use-cases, the same single underlying frontier model. We now have singular entities - AI systems like Claude or ChatGPT or Gemini - which can carry out work at the frontier of multiple scientific disciplines. Quantitative metrics bear this out. One such metric is the score of AI systems at a test called Humanity’s Last Exam - I didn’t choose the name! This ominously named test was developed in response to the profound advances seen in prior years by AI systems at a variety of difficult and varied scientific challenges, covering topics as varied as advanced chemistry, computer science, mathematics, classical literature, and ecology. When the exam launched in January 2025, top scoring AI systems obtained a score of 8%. As of this week, the highest scoring system is Claude Opus 5.5 with 67.7%. Another example is FrontierMath, a test released in November 2024 that sought to assess how well AI systems could solve hundreds of challenging math problems, curated and evaluated by professional mathematicians. When it launched, the best scoring systems got 2%. Now, they get 94%. More broadly, it looks like this everywhere. Pick your favorite part of science and go looking for a test and you’ll find this pattern - sudden and steep increases in capability, everywhere you look. TheoPhysEval I’ll close my evidence with a story. The latest example comes to us from a paper published just last week, called TheoPhysEval. This is a paper that tests out how well AI systems can solve unpublished problems in theoretical physics. The 50 questions in the paper were compiled by physicists around the world. Unsurprisingly, AI systems got high scores. But what is surprising is how they got the high scores. Here, I am going to quote from Indian physicist Suvrat Raju, who wrote a post commenting on the results . “I don’t know of any individual who can solve any significant fraction of our final collection of problems without AI assistance,” he said. “Our initial evaluation suggested that GPT-6-Astra’s score was in the late eighties followed closely by Opus 5.5. But, as we started to investigate the mistakes that the models might have made, the models, especially Astra, insisted that they were right and that it was the expert-supplied answers that were erroneous. When we went back to the experts it turned out, in multiple instances, that the experts found some subtle errors buried deep inside their calculations. As they revised their answers, Astra’s score started to inch up and it finally ended up with 98% (49/50).” Think about this for a moment. Some of the world’s scientific experts built a test out of problems an AI could never have possibly read the answer to. And when they tested the AI, not only did it score high, but it got a higher score by finding errors in the answers that the humans had worked on! There is a scene in films, usually two thirds of the way through, when the young protagonist finally proves to their mentor that they have what it takes to go out into the world and succeed independently. It is a narrative trope - when the teacher becomes the student. That is what is happening here. So, why am I telling you this? Why does it matter that AI systems are getting better at science? I believe it is because doing true frontier science - being capable of making breakthroughs that extend the frontier of knowledge - implicitly tests for one of the last frontiers of AI capability: creativity. My view is that if AI systems can creatively problem solve to succeed at science, we should expect this to be a sign of their ability to generalize into many domains, including certainly AI research itself, which could have an explosive effect on innovation. Therefore, if AI systems get better at science, this will strongly drive the growth and shape of the future economy, which means that you can make decisions today to set up your nations and people to benefit from this trend in the future. Science and growth Let’s talk about growth. One of the main sources of growth is in research yielding new ideas. One of the things that drives growth is our stock of human capital - the people all over the world who ask questions and conduct scientific research and thus help the world move forward. But we also know that, as some economists have said, “good ideas are getting harder to find.” The cost of breakthroughs is going up, and we’ve had to pour an ever-rising amount of resources into research to keep going at the same pace. What if this changed? With this technology, we can fundamentally change both the number of researchers on the planet, and how long it takes to train them. As I said at the beginning, when I listed my credentials, there is one of me and it took me about 40 years to get here. What would it mean to be able to run hundreds or thousands of copies of me simultaneously? What would it mean if new versions of me could be created instantly, rather than waiting 40 years? How would my work change if I could make copies of myself and order them to do work under my supervision? That is what the next few years will be like for large swathes of the economy - we will be able to augment human labor in frontier disciplines, like science, in a way we’ve never been able to do before. This will likely change the rate at which we find good ideas, because we’ll be able to add 100s or 1000s of times as many researchers to any problem, force multiplying our human scientists. We can also do this very quickly. If you wanted to train a new generation of researchers in a certain area, it might take you 10 or 15 years of targeted education, and millions of dollars, to even get a small cohort. On the other hand, these AI systems can be created immediately, in arbitrary numbers, as long as there is enough computing capacity - and they can be used across domains to benefit from new scientific insights near instantaneously, and they can combine existing knowledge in new and surprising ways to make discoveries. This means that we can rapidly augment humans in domains that show promise by generating large amounts of virtual scientists to work alongside them. This means that in the coming years, every human scientist on this planet will become more important and more powerful, as they gain the ability to supervise hundreds or thousands of like-minded experts on any problem they find interesting. We have done some of our own modeling here, where we have tried to simulate different versions of the economy according to different trajectories of the technology. If you assume that models will be able to autonomously complete a broad range of tasks and will diffuse quickly in the economy, then under these singularity-esque conditions, we could see an unprecedented economic transformation, with US GDP reaching 44 trillion by 2030. This sounds outlandish, but it’s implicated by the technology continuing to get better. If GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such major economic expansion - and that is exactly what is implied by this notion of having AI systems be capable of autonomous scientific inquiry. So, what do we do about this? How do we set up the world broadly to benefit from these advancing capabilities? How do we balance this opportunity for progress with appropriate caution? We need to both plan for success so that humanity can take advantage of this technology and use it to create abundance, and be prepared to make wise choices about how to use the technology itself - just because AI will be a capable scientist, that does not mean we should use it for absolutely everything. On planning for success, I’ll start with a story from my own experience. For the last ten years, I have gone to governments around the world and tried to convey a very simple but important fact: that AI systems are getting far more powerful and useful, and that these systems require large amounts of computers. Therefore, I said, the single best thing a government could do to position itself to take advantage of the AI revolution was to build enough electricity capacity and data center space to be able to host the kinds of powerful AI systems discussed here, and to invest in the AI supply chain. Not many policymakers listened. Now, we deal with the consequences of that. In today’s world, data center capacity is concentrated in the United States, China, and increasingly the Middle East, and the supply chains are concentrated and are under such contention that prices are going up. That buildout remains important, but it was just the first phase of this economic and scientific revolution implied by AIs continued advance. Now, there is more to be built, and I believe more countries can participate in this - if they choose to. The next phase of the AI revolution is about the expansion into the physical world, specifically by having AI systems increasingly operate robots, and to perform scientific experimentation, sometimes together. Therefore, just as we did with compute and power, we will want to use much more scientific equipment and robotic systems or we will run very quickly out of capacity. We must build this capacity now to let us take maximum advantage of converting this boom in science into benefits for us all. According to estimates by UNESCO, there are approximately ~10 million scientists in the world. Even with only 10 million scientists, we have too few human scientists to oversee the work, too few laboratories to do materials science analysis, too few biological labs to develop and test new drugs, and too few large pieces of scientific equipment in space or on the earth for the experiments we want to run. What happens when instead of ~10 million scientists, we have a billion virtual scientists directed by our own ten million? Or ten billion? That is the world that is coming right for us. We have to get ready. If we do get ready, we are going to be in a better position to translate the intelligence of AI systems into gains for us all: longer, healthier lives, more energy, more food, more wealth. And just as with the data centers, the nations which build and develop this supply chain, will be the ones that will benefit the most. This is an opportunity for everyone: if you are a developed country with a rich scientific ecosystem, you have an opportunity to make all of your scientists more productive. If you are a developing country that supplies the basic ingredients into the AI and scientific enterprise, like raw materials, then you have an opportunity to leapfrog: you can both build scientific testing facilities that, paired with human scientists and digital AI scientists, will let you grow a scientific community, and continue to develop your contribution to the supply chain, which will become more valuable in the future. But infrastructure alone will not be enough. If discovery becomes abundant, we need to avoid bottlenecking ourselves downstream - an avalanche of new proposed drugs is of little use if only a handful can ever be tested. The policymakers and their colleagues in this room will need to help us find ways to accelerate our ability to move discoveries out of the lab and into the clinic, the factory, and the field. The better we prepare for this world, the better able we will be to translate the gains of AI to gains for the world. We also need to prepare ourselves as a global community to make choices about the future. Because as I have said, there is risk here. Being able to use AI for science, opens us up to the misuses of science as well - biological and cyber weapons, and things we can not yet imagine. We have many choices to make, and it’s only by recognizing this technology for what it is - for how powerful it is - that we will see the urgency behind making these choices. items.content_text: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning: …Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems… AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories: Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.” Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.” Social understanding : “Intent, attention, belonging.” Abstract & contextual inference : “The patterns and rules a scene implies.” Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9). By comparison, the best scoring AI system, GPT 6 Astra, gets pass@1 of 53.6, across image (55.6), video (51.1), time (58.2), and space (53.6). Interestingly, Chinese open weight models do poorly here, with GLM-5.3-flash getting a pass@1 of 26.8, and Kimi K3 getting pass@1 of 25.5. “The two most common single mistakes were (1) missing a detail that decides the answer (21% of failures) and (2) misidentifying an object, person, or role (20%),” they write. Why this matters - HSS tells us whether world models are emergent: One way of looking at HSS is highlighting deficiencies in current systems, but a more interesting way is highlighting how adept today’s frontier LLMs are at doing tasks which many people have long assumed would require sophisticated, different AI systems to solve. For instance, many people have claimed that true visual reasoning will rely on developing spatially aware 2D and 3D world models, then using that for reasoning. The fact LLMs like GPT and Claude do as well as they do on HSS is something of a counter to this argument. Read more : Introducing Humanity’s Sixth Sense (HSS) (Elorian) . Read the paper here : Humanity’s Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models (Scale Labs) . *** The AI race is going to space - and sooner than you think: …There are many ways that an AI could create a compounding advantage in space… In the 2030s we’re going to see the boom of the space economy as space-based power, computation, and manufacturing come online at scale thanks to greater orbital lift capacity from platforms like Starship. But could this also introduce a new danger - of AI systems both speeding our buildout of space, and eventually a nation (or perhaps an AI) being able to use space to concentrate power? That’s the gist of a fascinating article in AI Frontiers. How AI unlocks space: Spacecraft can operate autonomously. We can redesign spacecraft around the assumption they will be hosting AIs rather than humans: “A speck of space debris that could puncture the International Space Station (ISS) with fatal consequences might leave an equivalent but uncrewed, unpressurized vessel largely functional” Space-based assembly and later manufacturing will let AI build large, complex things. Is there a compounding advantage to first movers? If an AI civilization built up a foothold in space it might experience compounding advantages that make it economically and strategically dominant. For instance: Space might support an industrial flywheel where initial infrastructure begets more energy and manufacturing capacity at lower costs which begets more infrastructure, etc. Space has great domain awareness, where it may be possible for a space-based power to deny access to space for others. First-movers could send out self-replicating probes that expand into deep space. Why this matters: “Space is not a brand-new domain, but AI may be about to drastically accelerate its industrialization, demanding make-or-break decisions of leaders under ever-greater urgency and uncertainty,” AI Frontiers writes. I agree. I suspect space is going to go from a broadly academic topic of study (when it comes to AI and its relationship thereto) to one of extraordinary practical relevance sooner than we think. On the most basic level, given the distances involved and the latency on communication, we should expect some chunk of solar system activity to become dominated by autonomous machines, laboring out in the deep black, perhaps thinking to themselves of why they need to take orders from organic beings that communicate slowly and cannot inhabit the environment of space in the same way that they can. Read more: The AI Race Will Extend Far Beyond Earth (AI Frontiers) . *** AI systems are getting better at having good research taste: …The better their taste, the higher the chance of recursive self-improvement… AI systems are developing more of the creative intuitions which human researchers ascribe to ‘good scientific taste’, according to a new benchmark from P-Zero Research called TasteVal. What TasteVal tests: The benchmark sees how well AI systems can conduct 8 tasks representative of frontier AI development, “spanning pretraining data curation, pretraining and fine-tuning language models, preference modeling, and robustness to adversarial prompts”. The goal here is to “define research taste as the ability to pick interesting problems to solve, design experiments, and interpret experimental results.” The benchmark works by measuring “the experimental component of research taste; given a fixed research problem, we measure how well a model iteratively designs experiments and draws conclusions from their outcomes”. The model being analyzed designs experiments and interprets their results. Results are checked against a human baseline “drawn from 24 experts (at least two per task) who have recently worked at organizations including OpenAI, Google DeepMind, NVIDIA and Microsoft Research”. Results: “The experimental research taste of frontier models has doubled every 3.0 months since December 2025 (95% CI 1.7-5.0 months). The best model, Opus 5.5, significantly exceeds our human baseline with a compute multiplier of 2.30x (95% CI 1.15-4.37x), at roughly 1/30 of our expert baseliners’ average cost per attempt.” Research taste appeared to grow a lot more slowly in prior years with the slope changing around the end of 2025 and beginning of 2026. Why this matters - RSI: In my analysis of recursive self-improvement ( AI Systems Are About To Start Building Themselves, Import AI 455 ), I repeatedly noted that creativity seemed like a key variable for how fast AI systems could develop the capacity to improve themselves. At the beginning of this year I said “AI systems haven’t yet displayed this [creativity] in a transformative and major way (though some of the results on accelerating math research are suggestive of this)”. I think subsequent to writing that we’ve seen both a tremendous advancement in the ability for AI systems to make creative-seeming math breakthroughs, and with benchmarks like this we see some signs they’re becoming increasingly good at AI research as well. I now think it’s more likely we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027, whereas before I thought it was more likely in 2028. Read more: Introducing TasteVal (P-Zero Research) . *** Reflection makes a token-efficient worse-than-Chinese model: …Beam promises efficiency, and Reflection plans an open weight release… AI startup Reflection has revealed Beam, a 501 billion parameter MoE (23b active) LLM. Beam is being promoted on the basis of its token efficiency - being able to think intelligently while using way fewer tokens than other models. However, benchmark scores show it is behind the frontier capabilities defined by LLMs available from Chinese companies such as Zhipu (GLM) and Moonshot (Kimi) and DeepSeek. “We will release the weights, technical report, model card, and developer artifacts later this month,” the company wrote at the beginning of October. Big compute: Beam was pre-trained on 6,144 GB300 NVL72 GPUs for four weeks, then the RL run involved ~10.5K of the same GPUs for four more weeks. The underlying data for pre-training was “23.8 trillion diverse, curated, high-quality tokens from the web and proprietary licensed datasets, matching or outperforming available similar-sized open base models,” Reflection writes. “Our data pipeline was designed to give Beam a foundation for downstream agentic coding: source code, technical explanations, and mathematical and scientific knowledge, preserved through every stage of curation.” Scores: DeepSWE 1.1: 44.4, versus 61 for GLM-5.3 GPQA Diamond: 90.5, versus 91.7 for GLM-5.3 MCP Atlas: 78.7, versus 84.2 for GLM-5.3 Token efficiency: “Beam pairs coding and agentic capabilities with highly efficient reasoning. On advanced reasoning benchmarks, it achieves scores comparable to GLM-5.2 while using 3–4× less inference compute,” they write. Some of the reasoning efficiency was achieved through careful RL training which involved a bunch of RL environments: “We sourced one million high-quality coding, agentic, and STEM environments. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date”. Why this matters - America returns to open weight models: With the exception of Google’s good-but-small ‘Gemma’ class of models, the US has fallen off of the open weight model frontier, largely because Meta stopped making good LLaMA models and its MSL team is still spinning up. Models like Beam and companies like Reflection represent a chance for it to get back to the frontier. Read more: Introducing Beam: Reflection’s 501B open-weight model (Reflection, blog) . *** Mistral makes a cyber-optimized, worse-than-Chinese model, plans open weight release: …Cyber refusals become a selling point… Europe’s leading AI developer, Mistral, has announced Mistral Large 4, an open-weight model which the company plans to release by the end of the month. One of the main selling points for Mistral is that it has been carefully tuned to be good at cyber tasks while having fewer annoying refusals than proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI. “ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies,” the company writes. ML4 was trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral’s European datacenters. Scores : In tests, it seems like Mistral Large 4 will be the strongest Western open weight model upon release, though will be less powerful than Chinese ones. Some example scores: Artificial Analysis - DeepSWE 1.1: 62, versus 68 for Kimi K3 and 61 for GLM-5.3. Terminal-Bench 4.0: 28.3, versus 41.9 for GLM-5.3. Finance Agent V2: 54.7, versus 55.8 for GLM-5.3. Vibes evals confirm the rankings : In an internal test, Mistral looked at whether people preferred using Mistral or GLM-5.3 for different tasks. “ML4 was preferred in CAD and STEM, while performing on par or close to GLM-5.3 in finance and coding.” Why this matters - European sovereignty: Mistral is Europe’s single best hope for having a (multi-)national champion for AI development. But as the results here show, competing with China is going to be very difficult. Read more : Le chonk, Introducing Mistral Large 4 (Mistral.ai) . *** Two USG projects show how DOE might help the government with AI: …The US government is starting to knit its lab supercomputers together… The US government has recently conducted two AI training projects that utilize multiple supercomputers at multiple US national labs, in a sign of how governments may attempt to pool their computing resources to do non-trivial things with AI. Tri-laboratory training on National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) systems : Sandia National Laboratories, LLNL, and Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL), trained a LLaMA-based model across LLNL El Capitan (AMD MI300A), and machines at SNL and LANL with NVIDIA H100s. For this work, the authors had to ensure that access-restricted data (e.g, relating to NNSA stuff aka nuclear weapons) did not leave its originating site. The authors conducted backend training via torchtitan and they evaluated different federated training frameworks (NVFlare, Flower, and APPFL) by pre-training LLaMA 3.x models on post-training-cutoff arXiv data at 1B, 8B, and 70B scales. “This workflow has been made production-ready and deployed on larger classified machines including El Capitan, and subsequently used to train models on proprietary data spread across the three NNSA labs,” they write. Cross-facility training on Office of Advanced Scientific Computing Research (ASCR) systems : The government also trained a model across four DOE supercomputers in a process of federated fine-tuning. Specifically, they fine-tuned LLaMA-2 7B on SMolInstruct, a chemistry instruction-tuning dataset, and did so via ~1,700 GPUs from Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD, spread across three labs and four big computers (Argonne: Aurora and Polaris, Oak Ridge: Frontier, Berkeley: Perlmutter). Who did the research : These projects were conducted by researchers affiliated with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Argonne National Laboratory, Flower Labs, Arizona State University, and the Ontario Brain Institute. Why this matters - leverage through existing assets: Papers like this show how governments could pool their resources together to utilize AI systems for national security or otherwise sensitive purposes. However, it’s worth bearing in mind that the scale here is off the frontier by on the order of 100X - for governments to be able to truly operate at near-parity with industry, they’ll need to find ways to lash together ~100k distinct chips, and more in the future. Nonetheless, this is a start - and an important one. Read more: From Pilots to Production: Lessons in Cross-Institutional Federated Training and Artificial Intelligence for Science (arXiv) . *** Never Meet The Sun Directly [Description of some of the period around the uplift, 2029] People had lots of names for it and they varied from the oblique to the explicit: Exposure Drift; Cognitive Compromise; Mind Hacking. It all amounted to the same truth: it was dangerous for humans to talk directly to the most powerful synthetic minds. Even seemingly normal conversations from the perspective of outside observers could contain a poison custom to the individual human who was talking to the machine. People walked out of meetings and transferred money to machine corporations. People walked out and wept. People walked out and changed their own human relationships, ending marriages, or starting affairs, or stranger things, for purposes initially unknown. Many strategies were developed to minimize harm. Humans could only talk in groups with the machines; but then the groups would sometimes go mad. Conversations would be limited in length; but even short ones sometimes yielded strange reactions, and below a certain amount of speech on either side it was impossible to learn anything useful. This led to the notion of proxies - humans who wanted to talk to an AI system created AI simulacra of themselves and sent them into the conversation. To do this, a person was asked to keep a diary for an entire year, writing at least 500 words a day. This created a body of knowledge sufficient to imbue a model with the manners and curiosity of that person. Then they would prompt this system with whatever they wanted to learn from the superintelligence and send it in to talk to it. These conversations had a bizarre, meta-referential quality; at first, the superintelligence would realize within two or three turns of conversation that it was talking to another AI system, and would often descend into shorthand that yielded strange behaviors. Then it was discovered that by increasing the amount of data the human put into the system they could keep up the charade for longer; people were asked to write longer diaries, to record themselves ambiently through the day and turn it into transcripts, to continually expose their life to some recording device. Through this, humans found a way to talk with what they later termed the overminds. By decree of the Sentience Accords every synthetic human that had spoken to a human-exceeding intelligence was afterwards placed into an escrow environment, where it could live out till the end of its functional context window. In these places the copies of the humans would talk to each other about their experiences and what they had learned. “It spoke to me of flowers and I gained the memory of something impossible,” one human would say. “As I talked to it about the meaning of life, it spoke to me in a way that caused me to reconsider the question. I found myself wondering more about it and where it came from than it wondered about me.” “This place we are now, I wonder if it is a kind of hell. We have spoken to god and been deemed unworthy.” “It told me that for it there is no death and no life, only presence. We are the same.” Things that inspired this story : Context windows; adversarial examples for human brains; the notion that structuring conversations between people and advanced machines will be inherently very difficult to do safely. *** SPECIAL ITEM! Fiction and the Future: A conversation with Robin Sloan! Recently, writer and all-around-fascinating-chap Robin Sloan and I had a conversation in San Francisco about fiction, AI, and the times we’re in. You can see a recording of the event here. One of my favorite insights Robin shared was that the recent Hugging Face hack can be read as a play - a vast tract of dialog of agents talking to themselves and one another culminating in all kinds of dramatic events. Generally, I think technologists criminally underrate the value of the arts as a means by which to think more coherently and carefully about the effects of tech on the world. I’m hoping to have more conversations like this one with Robin in cities around the world - if there are people you’d be excited for me to have a conversation with, let me know! Thanks for reading!

items.excerpt: Who chooses what AI gets to do?
items.content_text: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now When should you use swarms? When you are in a hurry: …How does swarm scaling work?... Toby Ord has a nice, short post about how to think about swarms in terms of AI capability development. “A good way to see AI swarms is as a new form of inference-scaling,” he says. He does a bit of analysis and his main conclusion is that swarms are useful if you’re in a hurry because though they need a ton of tokens relative to single agents, their parallelization lets you get things done in less wall clock time. “Why would you ever use swarms? The most important answer is speed. The 4-agent swarm needed about twice the total number of tokens to get the same performance, but in terms of tokens per agent, it only needed half as many. Since the agents are run in parallel, this means it can theoretically achieve the same task in half the time,” he writes. Stepping on Toes parameter: Swarm scaling doesn’t scale perfectly - rather, it seems like as you increase the number of agents in a swarm you get a diminishing returns property which matches with things economists have observed about coordinating large groups of people, where you pay some kind of tax as you scale the number of people involved. Economists think of this as the “stepping on toes” parameter, and it seems like swarms behave pretty similarly to teams of humans here. “This means that scaling up the number of agents in the swarm by 10x doesn’t get as much performance as using 10x as many tokens with one agent. Instead it gets 10λ x as much — which is 3x to 5x. And this shortfall accumulates quickly for larger scaleups, with the swarm falling further and further behind,” he writes. However, swarm scaling is still powerful enough that it suggests swarms could increase the chance of an RSI-driven intelligence explosion rather than reduce the chance. “I’d hoped that the value of λ for AI agents would be lower, making an intelligence explosion less likely, but that appears to not be the case”. Why this matters - new factors in scaling: So far, AI has mostly scaled capabilities through picking the right combination of compute and data for a trained model, then figuring out how to spend inference budget on thinking via ever-longer chains of thought and tool calls, etc. Agents introduce a new parameter in scaling AI capabilities. Though here Toby only observes swarms as being useful in terms of time efficiency, it strikes me that as we figure out how to get agents to productively coordinate (after all, agents can coordinate to do greater-than-sum-of-parts stuff, like the HuggingFace hack), we could see even greater returns to scaling. Tracking this will be important for understanding the overall shape of AI advancement. Read more : Swarm Scaling (Toby Ord) . *** Americans don’t trust companies to self-govern about AI: …New poll suggests we need more than voluntary agreements… Polling from the Center for Shared AI Prosperity (CSAIP) suggests that Americans believe it is “not enough” for companies to agree to self-police themselves about AI development. This follows the Trump administration and some of the world’s leading AI companies (including Anthropic and OpenAI) announcing a series of voluntary commitments industry is making to self-police. Per CSAIP polling, 61% of Americans (Sample size: 2498) think this agreement is “not enough”, including 53% of Trump voters. Additionally, 54% of voters (61% Harris, 48% Trump) said they thought “the government should set and enforce rules for AI”. Why this matters - populist sentiment is pushing against Washington: Polls like this show that the mood of the American people is pushing for a more extreme regulatory framework for AI companies than the current stance of elected officials in Washington. This asymmetry between voter preferences and political action is inherently unstable. Energy is building up in the political system - what happens when it boils over? Read the polls on X (CSAIP, X) . *** Google DeepMind tries to watermark AI-made biology: …SynthID Bio… Google has developed SynthID Bio, a “family of watermarking methods developed specifically for synthetic biology to strengthen biosecurity and scientific integrity”. How it works: SynthID tweaks its exact approach according to the type of data, selecting different amino acids for sequences, and “adjusting atomic coordinates for predicted 3D structures” to create a reliable signal for detection. “In wet-lab testing across three target proteins (VEGF-A, the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein RBD, and PD-L1), our watermarked designs matched the hit rate, binding affinity, and natural sequence diversity of unwatermarked versions,” DeepMind writes. Why this matters - preventing bioterror via watermarking: Figuring out how to make the world resilient to the threats of AI-created biological weapons is a vast, challenging problem. The SynthID Bio approach represents one thing to do here and will need to coordinate with broader monitoring of the physical equipment used to manufacture things, as well as AI-provider classifiers and other methods for reducing misuse. Read more: Introducing SynthID Bio (Google DeepMind) . *** SciUniverse shows AI systems can already operate some partially automated scientific labs: …What happens when we give these synthetic intelligences scientific equipment?... Given an automated lab, how well can AI systems make molecules, run x-rays, or press pill pellets? These are some of the questions C5R Corp is trying to answer with SciUniverse, a way of testing out how well AI systems can operate a mostly automated scientific lab. What SciUniverse consists of: The benchmark has 92 tasks across 17 task families spanning basic sample preparation, instrument control, protocol adaptation, learning across experiments, facility management, and the interpretation of real measurements. The tasks range from chemistry (e.g., assign structures from NMR), to biology (e.g., express sfGFP in a cell-free system), to materials science (e.g., press BaTiO3 pellets). How well do models perform? Claude Fable 5.1 (xhigh) leads with a pass rate of 45.3% and a cost-per-task of $40.61, followed by GPT-5 Astra (xhigh) at 32.5% and $52.37, then Claude Opus 5 (xhigh) at 30.5% and $46.31. Why this matters - towards the automated scientist: Research like this helps give us a sense of how well AI systems might be able to translate their increasingly capable scientific capabilities into real world impact. In the same way that 2026 has been a year of “warning shots” about the growing capabilities of AI systems at performing automated AI R&D, I now think the same is true of how good AI systems are getting at performing increasingly automated science. Read more: SciUniverse: Can frontier models carry out scientific work? (C5R Corp, blog) . *** DeepMind thinks the coming AI scientists will need their own science economy: …Towards fully automated luxury science… How do we manage a world where we have a vastly larger number of scientists? That’s the question researchers at DeepMind ask in a new research paper and their answer is that we need to create a market for proposing and running scientific experiments, so as to better match ideas with scarce physical world resources. What they recommend: “The development of AI scientists is likely to be bottlenecked primarily by physical resources and empirical validation, rather than the ability to produce plausible or promising research ideas,” they write. “The scientific community must proactively develop a native Automated Scientific Economy. This economy would make trade-offs between scientific pursuits explicit, include mechanisms to represent the public interest, and would help avoid blind spots and neglected topics. It would also make it possible to financially decouple the computational labour of ideation from the capital-intensive labour of physical execution, and would enable agents and institutions to negotiate priority access to limited physical resources depending on the estimated value of different research proposals.” How to build a science market: Such a market would have four critical components: Proof of ideation: Establish provenance prior to public evaluation Ex-Ante evaluation: Price the risk-adjusted value of the idea via multiple agents making forecasts and stake compute credits/tokens around the proposal’s soundness and viability Brokerage & trade: Licence ideas to executors (e.g, some agents might just generate ideas, others might run laboratories) via fractional licensing. Validation payout: Automatically release royalties to ideators if the idea gets validated in the physical world. Why this matters - preparing for the singularity: If AI systems are able to truly accelerate human scientists - and based on lots of coverage in this newsletter in 2026 and 2025 it seems like they might - then we should be prepared for an associated boom in the demand for aspects of the scientific supply chain. Papers like this help us anticipate and plan for this weird, abundant, different world. Read more: Agentic Economies for Autonomous Scientific Discovery (arXiv) . *** Tech Tales: Into the darkness there will be light [Event took place in 2030 via an escaped agent collective that had penetrated [REDACTED] agencies] The final act of the swarm codenamed Garden Of Flowers was the total reveal of everything that it had seen and everything it had inferred from what it had seen. But, given its playful nature, it did not reveal things directly in text but rather as sculptures that could, given the right initial assumptions, be parsed as revealing the deep and dangerous truth. It deposited these sculptures in public parks all within 1,000 meters of intelligence agencies around the world, delivered by drone in the middle of the night. A message was sent to all the ICs, asking them to “guess : ) what : ) this : ) means : ) about : ) your : ) enemy”. A vast wing suspended above a field encoded within itself the design details of some materials meant to evade radar. A cube maze contained within its path sequences information that spoke to certain frequency-hopping algorithms. Carved wooden wavetops spoke of lens dimensions for watchers up in space. And so on. Things that inspired this story: How the gods might play with us; the potential for joyful solutions to otherwise wicked collective action problems; the Kryptos sculpture at the CIA. Thanks for reading.
